Extend the approach to languages beyond English.
papers.abstract: Language models have been shown to be very effective in predicting brain recordings of subjects experiencing complex language stimuli. For a deeper understanding of this alignment, it is important to understand the correspondence between the detailed processing of linguistic information by the human brain versus language models. We investigate this correspondence via a direct approach, in which we eliminate information related to specific linguistic properties in the language model representations and observe how this intervention affects the alignment with fMRI brain recordings obtained while participants listened to a story. We investigate a range of linguistic properties (surface, syntactic, and semantic) and find that the elimination of each one results in a significant decrease in brain alignment. Specifically, we find that syntactic properties (i.e. Top Constituents and Tree Depth) have the largest effect on the trend of brain alignment across model layers. These findings provide clear evidence for the role of specific linguistic information in the alignment between brain and language models, and open new avenues for mapping the joint information processing in both systems. We make the code publicly available [https://github.com/subbareddy248/linguistic-properties-brain-alignment].

papers.title: Attention weights accurately predict language representations in the brain
papers.research_question: Are attention weights in Transformer-based language models related to language representations in the brain? Can attention weights predict brain responses to language stimuli?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights from Transformer-based language models accurately predict brain responses in language-related cortical areas, and contain information not captured by lexical or contextual embeddings.
papers.conclusion: Attention weights in Transformer-based LMs capture information that is reflected in brain representations during language processing, and indicate cortical areas that could be involved in integrating context across words.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 accurately predict brain responses in frontal and temporal cortices associated with language processing.
Attention weights better predict brain responses than lexical embeddings in many language-related areas.
Attention weights from middle layers of BERT explain the most variance in brain responses, consistent with linguistic relevance of middle layers.
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 perform similarly in predicting brain responses, suggesting consistency across unidirectional and bidirectional models.
In some cortical areas, attention weights predict brain responses better than contextual embeddings, indicating additional information in attention weights.
papers.limitation:
The temporal resolution of fMRI (2s) does not capture all the rapid changes in human speech.
Analyses were limited to English language comprehension.
The analyses demonstrate similarity of representations between Transformer-based LMs and brain responses, but do not directly prove the existence of similar underlying computational mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply the methods to other languages to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of context integration in the brain and in artificial neural networks.

Compare the results of our method of computing attention weights with more cognitively-inspired methods to provide more specific insights into how attention weights in Transformer-based LMs relate to processes in the human brain.
papers.abstract: In Transformer-based language models (LMs) the attention mechanism converts token embeddings into contextual embeddings that incorporate information from neighboring words. The resulting contextual hidden state embeddings have enabled highly accurate models of brain responses, suggesting that the attention mechanism constructs contextual embeddings that carry information reflected in language-related brain representations. However, it is unclear whether the attention weights that are used to integrate information across words are themselves related to language representations in the brain. To address this question we analyzed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) recordings of participants reading English language narratives. We provided the narrative text as input to two LMs (BERT and GPT-2) and extracted their corresponding attention weights. We then used encoding models to determine how well attention weights can predict recorded brain responses. We find that attention weights accurately predict brain responses in much of the frontal and temporal cortices. Our results suggest that the attention mechanism itself carries information that is reflected in brain representations. Moreover, these results indicate cortical areas in which context integration may occur.

papers.title: Finding Structure in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to humans, and how can such structures be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that language models capture abstract linguistic structure similar to humans, and develops interpretability techniques to reveal this structure. It shows that models exhibit structural priming, generalize from indirect evidence, and that interpretability methods must be evaluated with care.
papers.conclusion: The thesis provides a detailed account of grammatical knowledge in language models and offers directions for using computational methods to investigate linguistic questions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit human-like structural priming effects, indicating they capture abstract syntactic structure.
Language models can generalize linguistic patterns from indirect evidence, as shown by filtered corpus training experiments.
Interpretability methods for feature interaction detection vary in faithfulness and must be evaluated carefully.
Language models use monotonicity information to predict negative polarity item licensing.
Adjective order preferences in language models are influenced by data statistics and cognitive factors.
papers.abstract: When we speak, write or listen, we continuously make predictions based on our knowledge of a language's grammar. Remarkably, children acquire this grammatical knowledge within just a few years, enabling them to understand and generalise to novel constructions that have never been uttered before. Language models are powerful tools that create representations of language by incrementally predicting the next word in a sentence, and they have had a tremendous societal impact in recent years. The central research question of this thesis is whether these models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to that of humans. This question lies at the intersection of natural language processing, linguistics, and interpretability. To address it, we will develop novel interpretability techniques that enhance our understanding of the complex nature of large-scale language models. We approach our research question from three directions. First, we explore the presence of abstract linguistic information through structural priming, a key paradigm in psycholinguistics for uncovering grammatical structure in human language processing. Next, we examine various linguistic phenomena, such as adjective order and negative polarity items, and connect a model's comprehension of these phenomena to the data distribution on which it was trained. Finally, we introduce a controlled testbed for studying hierarchical structure in language models using various synthetic languages of increasing complexity and examine the role of feature interactions in modelling this structure. Our findings offer a detailed account of the grammatical knowledge embedded in language model representations and provide several directions for investigating fundamental linguistic questions using computational methods.

papers.title: Learning Music Helps You Read: Using Transfer to Study Linguistic Structure in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does training on non-linguistic data with latent structure (like music or code) affect the ability of LSTMs to model natural language, and what structural features are being transferred?
papers.core_contribution: LSTMs can learn generalizable structural features from non-linguistic data (music, code) and transfer them to natural language, and hierarchical recursion is not necessary for this transfer; flat head-dependent pair structure is equally effective. Transfer between natural languages is correlated with syntactic typological similarity.
papers.conclusion: LSTMs can learn and transfer structural features from non-linguistic data to natural language, and simple head-dependent pair structure (not necessarily hierarchical) is sufficient for such transfer, suggesting recursion may not be as central to language learning as previously thought.
papers.key_findings:
Training on non-linguistic structured data (music, code) improves transfer to natural language compared to random baselines.
Training on artificial languages with nested hierarchical structure (Nesting Parentheses) and flat paired structure (Flat Parentheses) both lead to similar gains, indicating that recursion is not necessary for transfer.
Transfer performance between natural languages is highly correlated with typological syntactic similarity (WALS-syntax distance).
Vocabulary distribution (Zipfian) alone provides minor gains but structural features are far more important.
The TILT method provides a way to analyze structural inductive biases in language models.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to LSTM models; it is unknown if the results generalize to Transformer architectures.
The typological distance metric is based on only 49 syntactic features and may not be perfectly accurate.
future_direction: Test if the results hold on Transformer architectures.
Ablate specific structural features by creating hypothetical languages that differ in single grammatical features.
Test on structured data that's completely unrelated to language, such as images.
papers.abstract: We propose transfer learning as a method for analyzing the encoding of grammatical structure in neural language models. We train LSTMs on non-linguistic data and evaluate their performance on natural language to assess which kinds of data induce generalizable structural features that LSTMs can use for natural language. We find that training on non-linguistic data with latent structure (MIDI music or Java code) improves test performance on natural language, despite no overlap in surface form or vocabulary. To pinpoint the kinds of abstract structure that models may be encoding to lead to this improvement, we run similar experiments with two artificial parentheses languages: one which has a hierarchical recursive structure, and a control which has paired tokens but no recursion. Surprisingly, training a model on either of these artificial languages leads to the same substantial gains when testing on natural language. Further experiments on transfer between natural languages controlling for vocabulary overlap show that zero-shot performance on a test language is highly correlated with typological syntactic similarity to the training language, suggesting that representations induced by pre-training correspond to the cross-linguistic syntactic properties. Our results provide insights into the ways that neural models represent abstract syntactic structure, and also about the kind of structural inductive biases which allow for natural language acquisition.

papers.title: Language Models Learn POS First
papers.research_question: How and when are linguistic structures, such as part-of-speech tagging and global topic information, acquired during the training of language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that during training, language models acquire part-of-speech tagging early and global topic information continuously, using methods like gradient concentration and SVCCA.
papers.conclusion: Early training focuses on learning part-of-speech syntax for initial performance, while later training shifts to refining global topic representations for further gains.
papers.key_findings:
Frequent words have more concentrated gradients, and concentration increases over time during training.
Closed POS classes (e.g., pronouns, prepositions) show early concentration stabilization, while open classes (e.g., nouns, verbs) continue to become more concentrated.
Part-of-speech tagging is learned early in training, with representation peaking before the first optimizer step size rescale.
Global topic information is learned continuously throughout training, with representation increasing over time.
future_direction: Develop ways of interpreting syntactic structures during training.
papers.abstract: A glut of recent research shows that language models capture linguistic structure. Such work answers the question of whether a model represents linguistic structure. But how and when are these structures acquired? Rather than treating the training process itself as a black box, we investigate how representations of linguistic structure are learned over time. In particular, we demonstrate that different aspects of linguistic structure are learned at different rates, with part of speech tagging acquired early and global topic information learned continuously.

papers.title: Contextual Feature Extraction Hierarchies Converge in Large Language Models and the Brain
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to the alignment of large language models (LLMs) with the brain's language processing mechanisms, and do LLMs share fundamental computational principles that increasingly align with the spoken language processing pathway in the human brain?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that higher-performing large language models (LLMs) exhibit greater alignment with the brain's hierarchical language processing, and that contextual information is a key factor driving this convergence.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that hierarchical structure and contextual dependencies are fundamental to language processing, leading to convergent strategies in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Higher-performing LLMs achieve higher peak brain similarity scores.
Better-performing LLMs peak in brain similarity at earlier layers compared to lower-performing models.
Better-performing LLMs have hierarchical feature extraction pathways that more closely align with the brain's hierarchy.
Contextual information is crucial for brain similarity and hierarchy alignment, with long context windows being particularly important.
Top-performing LLMs converge in their feature extraction hierarchies, as shown by high inter-model similarity.
papers.limitation:
Limited iEEG coverage may not capture all relevant brain regions.
The speech comprehension task is simple and may not fully engage higher-level language processing.
LLMs are trained for next-word prediction, which differs from the comprehension task performed by subjects.
future_direction: Using brain similarity as an evaluation metric for LLM development.
Improving contextual processing in LLMs to enhance performance and brain alignment.
Investigating the role of later layers in LLMs for higher-order integration.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have sparked interest in the parallels between large language models (LLMs) and human neural processing, particularly in language comprehension. While prior research has established similarities in the representation of LLMs and the brain, the underlying computational principles that cause this convergence, especially in the context of evolving LLMs, remain elusive. Here, we examined a diverse selection of high-performance LLMs with similar parameter sizes to investigate the factors contributing to their alignment with the brain's language processing mechanisms. We find that as LLMs achieve higher performance on benchmark tasks, they not only become more brain-like as measured by higher performance when predicting neural responses from LLM embeddings, but also their hierarchical feature extraction pathways map more closely onto the brain's while using fewer layers to do the same encoding. We also compare the feature extraction pathways of the LLMs to each other and identify new ways in which high-performing models have converged toward similar hierarchical processing mechanisms. Finally, we show the importance of contextual information in improving model performance and brain similarity. Our findings reveal the converging aspects of language processing in the brain and LLMs and offer new directions for developing models that align more closely with human cognitive processing.

papers.title: Llama See, Llama Do: A Mechanistic Perspective on Contextual Entrainment and Distraction in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do language models become distracted by irrelevant contextual information, and what is the mechanistic basis for this distraction?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies contextual entrainment, a novel phenomenon where LMs assign higher probabilities to tokens that appear in the context, and discovers entrainment heads that control this effect, providing a mechanistic perspective on distraction.
papers.conclusion: Contextual entrainment is a novel mechanistic phenomenon that plays a crucial role in LM distraction, and interpretability techniques can provide insights for real-world applications such as RAG.
papers.key_findings:
LMs assign significantly higher logits/probabilities to tokens that have appeared in the context prompt, even for random tokens (contextual entrainment).
The magnitude of contextual entrainment is influenced by semantic factors, with counterfactual prompts having a stronger effect than factual ones.
A small set of attention heads (entrainment heads) are responsible for contextual entrainment; disabling them attenuates the effect.
Entrainment heads are relation-specific, not model-specific.
Removing entrainment heads has minimal impact on other LM capabilities like factual recall and in-context learning.
papers.limitation:
Did not conduct experiments using larger LMs due to resource limitations.
Only used the LRE dataset and not standard RAG datasets.
Do not propose an application to mitigate the distraction problem.
future_direction: Reproduce results using larger models.
Validate findings using standard RAG datasets.
Further steps toward addressing the distraction problem.
papers.abstract: We observe a novel phenomenon, contextual entrainment, across a wide range of language models (LMs) and prompt settings, providing a new mechanistic perspective on how LMs become distracted by ``irrelevant'' contextual information in the input prompt. Specifically, LMs assign significantly higher logits (or probabilities) to any tokens that have previously appeared in the context prompt, even for random tokens. This suggests that contextual entrainment is a mechanistic phenomenon, occurring independently of the relevance or semantic relation of the tokens to the question or the rest of the sentence. We find statistically significant evidence that the magnitude of contextual entrainment is influenced by semantic factors. Counterfactual prompts have a greater effect compared to factual ones, suggesting that while contextual entrainment is a mechanistic phenomenon, it is modulated by semantic factors. We hypothesise that there is a circuit of attention heads -- the entrainment heads -- that corresponds to the contextual entrainment phenomenon. Using a novel entrainment head discovery method based on differentiable masking, we identify these heads across various settings. When we ``turn off'' these heads, i.e., set their outputs to zero, the effect of contextual entrainment is significantly attenuated, causing the model to generate output that capitulates to what it would produce if no distracting context were provided. Our discovery of contextual entrainment, along with our investigation into LM distraction via the entrainment heads, marks a key step towards the mechanistic analysis and mitigation of the distraction problem.

papers.title: Unveiling Multilinguality in Transformer Models: Exploring Language Specificity in Feed-Forward Networks
papers.research_question: Do neurons in the feed-forward networks of multilingual transformer models exhibit language-specific or language-agnostic behavior across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that in multilingual transformer models, feed-forward network layers near the input and output are more language-specific, whereas middle layers are more language-agnostic.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that language specificity in FFNs is higher near the input and output layers, and training data imbalance influences detector activations.
papers.key_findings:
Layers closest to the input and output exhibit more language-specific behavior compared to middle layers.
The number of detectors triggered by English prefixes is higher than for Czech, reflecting training data imbalance.
The number of unique detectors varies across layers, with sparsity patterns observed in FFN activations.
Linear classifiers can predict the language of input prefixes from detector activations with higher accuracy in input and output layers.
Czech-specific detectors decrease in middle layers, suggesting semantic processing uses more language-agnostic detectors.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to only the XGLM model.
Study is centred on the Czech-English language pair, and findings may not generalize to other languages.
Lack of qualitative analysis of linguistic cues triggering detector activation.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more language pairs and other multilingual autoregressive language models.
papers.abstract: Recent research suggests that the feed-forward module within Transformers can be viewed as a collection of key-value memories, where the keys learn to capture specific patterns from the input based on the training examples. The values then combine the output from the 'memories' of the keys to generate predictions about the next token. This leads to an incremental process of prediction that gradually converges towards the final token choice near the output layers. This interesting perspective raises questions about how multilingual models might leverage this mechanism. Specifically, for autoregressive models trained on two or more languages, do all neurons (across layers) respond equally to all languages? No! Our hypothesis centers around the notion that during pretraining, certain model parameters learn strong language-specific features, while others learn more language-agnostic (shared across languages) features. To validate this, we conduct experiments utilizing parallel corpora of two languages that the model was initially pretrained on. Our findings reveal that the layers closest to the network's input or output tend to exhibit more language-specific behaviour compared to the layers in the middle.

papers.title: Using Shapley interactions to understand how models use structure
papers.research_question: How do language and speech models internally represent linguistic structure, and how can Shapley interactions reveal these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Shapley Taylor interaction indices (STII) can reveal how language and speech models encode linguistic structure, showing correlations with syntactic proximity, non-compositional semantics, and phonetic coarticulation.
papers.conclusion: Shapley interactions provide a powerful method for understanding how models encode structural relationships in data, spanning syntax, semantics, and phonetics, and highlight the importance of domain expertise for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Autoregressive language models (GPT-2) show a strong correlation between Shapley interaction strength and the syntactic proximity of input tokens.
Both autoregressive and masked language models (BERT) exhibit stronger Shapley interactions between tokens in multiword expressions (MWEs) with non-compositional, idiomatic meaning.
In speech models (wav2vec2), Shapley interactions are stronger between consonant-vowel pairs than between consonant-consonant pairs, reflecting the phonetic phenomenon of coarticulation.
Within consonants, more sonorant (vowel-like) consonants show higher interaction with surrounding phonemes than less sonorant consonants.
Shapley interaction strength decreases with increasing positional distance between tokens, indicating models treat distant context more like a bag of words.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to pairwise interactions and does not consider higher-order interactions.
The analysis is correlational and does not establish causal predictive power of Shapley interactions.
Experiments are conducted on relatively small models (e.g., GPT-2, BERT-base), not state-of-the-art production models.
In speech analysis, the exact duration of a phoneme is challenging to define, making boundary alignment approximate.
future_direction: Extend analysis to higher-order Shapley interactions to capture more complex hierarchical structures.
Apply the methodology to compare models with different architectures trained on the same objective.
Incorporate analysis of internal model features, not just input features.
Pursue interdisciplinary collaboration with domain experts (e.g., phonology, syntax) to guide interpretability research.
papers.abstract: Language is an intricately structured system, and a key goal of NLP interpretability is to provide methodological insights for understanding how language models represent this structure internally. In this paper, we use Shapley Taylor interaction indices (STII) in order to examine how language and speech models internally relate and structure their inputs. Pairwise Shapley interactions measure how much two inputs work together to influence model outputs beyond if we linearly added their independent influences, providing a view into how models encode structural interactions between inputs. We relate the interaction patterns in models to three underlying linguistic structures: syntactic structure, non-compositional semantics, and phonetic coarticulation. We find that autoregressive text models encode interactions that correlate with the syntactic proximity of inputs, and that both autoregressive and masked models encode nonlinear interactions in idiomatic phrases with non-compositional semantics. Our speech results show that inputs are more entangled for pairs where a neighboring consonant is likely to influence a vowel or approximant, showing that models encode the phonetic interaction needed for extracting discrete phonemic representations.

papers.title: Do Multilingual Neural Machine Translation Models Contain Language Pair Specific Attention Heads?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual neural machine translation models contain language pair specific attention heads? The paper investigates this by analyzing individual attention heads in a many-to-one NMT model.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that in a multilingual NMT model, the most important attention heads are largely language-independent, and about 30% of heads can be pruned without significant performance loss.
papers.conclusion: Although rare language-pair specific attention heads exist, the most important heads are language-independent, and around 30% of heads can be pruned without retraining and with almost no loss in BLEU.
papers.key_findings:
The set of most important attention heads is very similar across different language pairs.
It is possible to remove nearly one-third of the less important attention heads without greatly hurting translation quality.
For encoder-decoder (cross) attention heads, the coverage metric is a better indicator for pruning importance, while for encoder self-attention heads, the confidence metric is more effective.
Some rare attention heads are language-pair specific, as identified by the exhaustive Sequential Backward Selection (SBS) procedure.
The variance, confidence, and coverage metrics provide a proxy for head importance, but the SBS algorithm yields the best ranking for pruning.
future_direction: Perform pruning at different levels of granularity (beyond single scalar metrics) to identify which parts of the model are more language-specific.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on the analysis of the multilingual representations focus on identifying whether there is an emergence of languageindependent representations, or whether a multilingual model partitions its weights among different languages. While most of such work has been conducted in a "black-box" manner, this paper aims to analyze individual components of a multilingual neural translation (NMT) model. In particular, we look at the encoder self-attention and encoder-decoder attention heads (in a many-to-one NMT model) that are more specific to the translation of a certain language pair than others by (1) employing metrics that quantify some aspects of the attention weights such as "variance" or "confidence", and (2) systematically ranking the importance of attention heads with respect to translation quality. Experimental results show that surprisingly, the set of most important attention heads are very similar across the language pairs and that it is possible to remove nearly one-third of the less important heads without hurting the translation quality greatly.

papers.title: Interpreting Character Embeddings With Perceptual Representations: The Case of Shape, Sound, and Color
papers.research_question: What information is encoded in character embeddings and how do they correlate with perceptual representations of shape, sound, and color?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the use of perceptual representations (shape, sound, color) to evaluate character embeddings via representational similarity analysis and probing classifiers, finding that character embeddings correlate with sound for alphabetic scripts and shape for featural scripts, and that phonological information is encoded in the embeddings.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that character embeddings encode perceptual information and that representational similarity analysis and probing tasks are effective for intrinsic evaluation, with promising results for interpretability and cross-linguistic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Textual character representations correlate strongly with sound representations for languages using alphabetic scripts.
Shape representations correlate with character embeddings for featural scripts like Korean.
Phonological features such as voicing are encoded in both LSTM and transformer-based character embeddings, as shown by probing classifiers.
Correlation patterns vary across scripts and orthographic depths (e.g., Spanish, with shallow orthography, shows higher sound correlations).
Representational similarity analysis provides an intrinsic evaluation method for character embeddings, with results significantly above random baselines.
papers.limitation:
The probing task results are based on a limited number of examples (characters per language), which requires cautious interpretation.
The study includes only five languages; more languages and scripts are needed for generalizable insights.
future_direction: Include additional languages and scripts to identify more generalizable insights.
Use perceptual representations as pre-trained representations for tasks like grapheme-to-phoneme conversion or predicting orthographic errors.
Further dissect the differences between character language models (e.g., LSTM vs. transformer) in terms of the information they encode.
papers.abstract: Character-level information is included in many NLP models, but evaluating the information encoded in character representations is an open issue. We leverage perceptual representations in the form of shape, sound, and color embeddings and perform a representational similarity analysis to evaluate their correlation with textual representations in five languages. This cross-lingual analysis shows that textual character representations correlate strongly with sound representations for languages using an alphabetic script, while shape correlates with featural scripts. We further develop a set of probing classifiers to intrinsically evaluate what phonological information is encoded in character embeddings. Our results suggest that information on features such as voicing are embedded in both LSTM and transformer-based representations.

papers.title: Structured World Representations in Maze-Solving Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn to solve mazes and what internal representations do they form?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks learn linear representations of maze connectivity in their residual stream, and specific attention heads (adjacency heads) handle path-following by attending to valid neighbors.
papers.conclusion: Transformers acquire emergent linear representations of maze connectivity encoded in a single token's latent state, and their embedding layers learn spatial structure; specific attention heads are identified that respect maze topology.
papers.key_findings:
The residual stream of a single token (e.g., <PATH_START>) can be linearly decoded to reconstruct the entire maze structure.
The embedding layer learns an emergent spatial structure where distances between coordinate tokens correlate with Manhattan distances on the grid.
Specific attention heads (e.g., Layer 5, Head 3) consistently attend to tokens at path length 1 from the current position, acting as adjacency heads that respect maze topology.
The formation of linearly decodable maze representations coincides with grokking-like transitions where generalization performance improves sharply.
Models often violate maze constraints (e.g., pass through walls) but still reach the target, indicating imperfect learning of constraints.
papers.limitation:
The generalizability of findings from toy models to larger scales remains uncertain.
Models often violate maze constraints (e.g., pass through walls) even when reaching the target.
future_direction: Construct a more complete mechanistic picture of how elementary heads operate over the linear world model to form circuits for solving mazes.
Investigate the generality of emergent models by training different neural network architectures on the same tasks with different input representations.
papers.abstract: Transformer models underpin many recent advances in practical machine learning applications, yet understanding their internal behavior continues to elude researchers. Given the size and complexity of these models, forming a comprehensive picture of their inner workings remains a significant challenge. To this end, we set out to understand small transformer models in a more tractable setting: that of solving mazes. In this work, we focus on the abstractions formed by these models and find evidence for the consistent emergence of structured internal representations of maze topology and valid paths. We demonstrate this by showing that the residual stream of only a single token can be linearly decoded to faithfully reconstruct the entire maze. We also find that the learned embeddings of individual tokens have spatial structure. Furthermore, we take steps towards deciphering the circuity of path-following by identifying attention heads (dubbed $\textit{adjacency heads}$), which are implicated in finding valid subsequent tokens.

papers.title: Unsupervised Learning and Representation of Mandarin Tonal Categories by a Generative CNN
papers.research_question: Can a generative model learn Mandarin tonal categories without labeled data, and does it correspond to human acquisition stages?
papers.core_contribution: The ciwGAN model can learn Mandarin tonal categories unsupervised, and its learning pattern mirrors early stages of human tonal acquisition.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised generative models can learn complex tonal contrasts without labeled data, replicating human acquisition patterns and providing insights for interpretability in deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
The male-only ciwGAN model learned to consistently encode four Mandarin tonal categories using its categorical variables.
The whole-set model learned partial analogues to two tones (falling T4 and high T1), corresponding to early human acquisition stages.
Tonal representations are encoded in the later convolutional layers (Conv4 and Conv3) but not in earlier layers like Conv2.
Statistically significant differences in F0 trajectories were found across categorical variables for all trained models.
The model trained on male tokens showed the clearest tonal learning, with an adjusted R² of 0.12 approaching naturalistic data.
papers.limitation:
The female-set model struggled to learn consistent tonal categories despite having a wider F0 range, and the reason is unclear.
The whole-set model only learned partial tonal categories, not all four.
future_direction: Investigating more complex tonal alternations in future research.
Using the approach for neural comparison between tone learning in humans and artificial models.
papers.abstract: This paper outlines the methodology for modeling tonal learning in fully unsupervised models of human language acquisition. Tonal patterns are among the computationally most complex learning objectives in language. We argue that a realistic generative model of human language (ciwGAN) can learn to associate its categorical variables with Mandarin Chinese tonal categories without any labeled data. All three trained models showed statistically significant differences in F0 across categorical variables. The model trained solely on male tokens consistently encoded tone. Our results sug- gest that not only does the model learn Mandarin tonal contrasts, but it learns a system that corresponds to a stage of acquisition in human language learners. We also outline methodology for tracing tonal representations in internal convolutional layers, which shows that linguistic tools can contribute to interpretability of deep learning and can ultimately be used in neural experiments.

papers.title: Why Can GPT Learn In-Context? Language Models Implicitly Perform Gradient Descent as Meta-Optimizers
papers.research_question: What is the working mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) in GPT models? The paper investigates whether ICL can be understood as implicit finetuning, where the attention mechanism performs a form of gradient descent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent, leading to the understanding that in-context learning is a form of implicit finetuning. Inspired by this, the paper designs a momentum-based attention mechanism that improves performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning can be understood as implicit finetuning via a meta-optimization process, and this understanding can inspire model design, as demonstrated by the momentum-based attention.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer attention has a dual form with gradient descent, which explains in-context learning as implicit finetuning.
Empirical comparisons show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning in terms of predictions, attention outputs, attention weights, and attention to training tokens.
Momentum-based attention, designed by analogy with gradient descent with momentum, improves performance on language modeling and in-context learning tasks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Transformer-based models and does not consider other architectures.
The dual form is derived using a relaxed linear attention approximation, and the mechanism of standard attention without approximation may be more complex.
Experiments are limited to models up to 2.7B parameters and only classification tasks, leaving larger models and other task types for future work.
future_direction: Study in-context learning for non-Transformer architectures.
Investigate the mechanism of standard Transformer attention without the linear approximation.
Extend the analysis to larger models and other tasks like open-ended generation.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models have shown surprising in-context learning (ICL) ability. With a few demonstration input-label pairs, they can predict the label for an unseen input without parameter updates. Despite the great success in performance, its working mechanism still remains an open question. In this paper, we explain language models as meta-optimizers and understand in-context learning as implicit finetuning. Theoretically, we figure out that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent. On top of it, we understand ICL as follows: GPT first produces meta-gradients according to the demonstration examples, and then these meta-gradients are applied to the original GPT to build an ICL model. We comprehensively compare the behaviors of in-context learning and explicit finetuning on real tasks to provide empirical evidence that supports our understanding. Experimental results show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning from multiple perspectives. Inspired by the dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, we design a momentum-based attention by analogy with gradient descent with momentum. The improved performance over vanilla attention further supports our understanding from another perspective, and more importantly, shows the potential to utilize our understanding for future model design. The code is available at \url{https://aka.ms/icl}.

papers.title: Length Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How is output sequence length information encoded within the internal representations of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that output sequence length information is encoded in the multi-head attention mechanisms of lower transformer layers, and that scaling specific hidden units can control length while preserving text informativeness.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have constructed robust internal mechanisms for controlling output sequence length, with in-context learning performing similarly to implicit fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Length representations are strongly correlated with the second layer's attention outputs.
Specific hidden units in the attention mechanisms are highly activated for length control and become more active with length-specific prompts.
Scaling these length-related hidden units can adjust output sequence length without losing the informativeness of generated text.
Fine-tuning reinforces the model's reliance on these top-k length-related units for precise length control.
The same hidden units are activated in priming prompts across zero-shot and fine-tuned settings, indicating robust internal mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
Neural networks might decode functionally irrelevant information from model representations.
The proposed methods do not effectively control length in LLMs with grouped-query attentions in zero-shot settings.
It is unclear if the findings extend to models with Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures.
future_direction: Extend the approach to models with grouped-query attentions.
Investigate Mixture of Experts (MoE) models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities across various tasks, that are learned from massive amounts of text-based data. Although LLMs can control output sequence length, particularly in instruction-based settings, the internal mechanisms behind this control have been unexplored yet. In this study, we provide empirical evidence on how output sequence length information is encoded within the internal representations in LLMs. In particular, our findings show that multi-head attention mechanisms are critical in determining output sequence length, which can be adjusted in a disentangled manner. By scaling specific hidden units within the model, we can control the output sequence length without losing the informativeness of the generated text, thereby indicating that length information is partially disentangled from semantic information. Moreover, some hidden units become increasingly active as prompts become more length-specific, thus reflecting the model's internal awareness of this attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs have learned robust and adaptable internal mechanisms for controlling output length without any external control.

papers.title: What does it mean to be language-agnostic? Probing multilingual sentence encoders for typological properties
papers.research_question: How do multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties of languages, and how does this vary with different pretraining strategies?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties, but the encoding differs based on pretraining objectives: models with cross-lingual objectives (LASER, XLM) lose typological information in higher layers and create a shared interlingual space, while models with monolingual objectives (M-BERT, XLM-R) retain typological information in all layers and partition the space into language-specific subspaces.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between universality and language-specific information in multilingual encoders, and pretraining objectives influence how typological information is encoded.
papers.key_findings:
All encoders capture some typological properties (word order, pronouns, negation).
M-BERT and XLM-R outperform LASER and XLM on lexical and morphological properties.
Typological information is localizable in lower layers of LASER and XLM, but spread across all layers in M-BERT and XLM-R.
Cross-lingual training leads to more language-agnostic representations but at the cost of losing language-specific typological information in higher layers.
XLM generalizes to languages unseen during pretraining, capturing their typological properties.
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders have seen much success in cross-lingual model transfer for downstream NLP tasks. Yet, we know relatively little about the properties of individual languages or the general patterns of linguistic variation that they encode. We propose methods for probing sentence representations from state-of-the-art multilingual encoders (LASER, M-BERT, XLM and XLM-R) with respect to a range of typological properties pertaining to lexical, morphological and syntactic structure. In addition, we investigate how this information is distributed across all layers of the models. Our results show interesting differences in encoding linguistic variation associated with different pretraining strategies.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Language-Specific Neurons: The Key to Multilingual Capabilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models process multilingual texts, and what are the language-specific mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language activation probability entropy (LAPE) to identify language-specific neurons in LLMs, revealing that a small subset of neurons in top and bottom layers are crucial for multilingual processing and can be manipulated to steer output language.
papers.conclusion: The study provides evidence that language-specific neurons are key to multilingual capabilities in LLMs, and the LAPE method offers a way to identify and manipulate these neurons for better understanding and control.
papers.key_findings:
Deactivating language-specific neurons significantly impairs the model's proficiency in that language, as shown by increased perplexity and reduced generation quality.
Language-specific neurons are predominantly located in the bottom and top layers of LLMs, with bottom layers mapping inputs to a shared semantic space and top layers handling vocabulary mapping.
It is possible to steer the output language of LLMs by selectively activating or deactivating language-specific neurons, mitigating off-target language issues.
Low-resource languages are centered around high-resource languages in the representation space, indicating dominance relations.
Neurons in larger models tend to be more specialized for single languages rather than shared among multiple languages.
papers.limitation:
The LAPE method is relative to the presence of multiple languages and cannot establish an absolute threshold for single-language scenarios.
Criteria for distinguishing between high-resource and low-resource languages within the model need further investigation.
Managing a large number of languages and differences between various languages requires future research.
future_direction: Enhance knowledge transfer between major and minor languages.
Devise efficient strategies for continual pre-training to accommodate specific languages.
Investigate the differences between various languages in the model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable multilingual capabilities without being pre-trained on specially curated multilingual parallel corpora. It remains a challenging problem to explain the underlying mechanisms by which LLMs process multilingual texts. In this paper, we delve into the composition of Transformer architectures in LLMs to pinpoint language-specific regions. Specially, we propose a novel detection method, language activation probability entropy (LAPE), to identify language-specific neurons within LLMs. Based on LAPE, we conduct comprehensive experiments on several representative LLMs, such as LLaMA-2, BLOOM, and Mistral. Our findings indicate that LLMs' proficiency in processing a particular language is predominantly due to a small subset of neurons, primarily situated in the models' top and bottom layers. Furthermore, we showcase the feasibility to "steer" the output language of LLMs by selectively activating or deactivating language-specific neurons. Our research provides important evidence to the understanding and exploration of the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Abstraction Induces the Brain Alignment of Language and Speech Models
papers.research_question: Why do intermediate hidden states of language and speech models predict brain responses? Is this due to shared meaning abstraction rather than next-word prediction properties?
papers.core_contribution: The correspondence between speech/language models and the brain derives from shared meaning abstraction, not next-word prediction. The intrinsic dimension of representations peaks in intermediate layers and strongly predicts brain encoding performance.
papers.conclusion: Meaning abstraction, as captured by high intrinsic dimension, is the key driver of model-brain similarity, and prediction objectives alone are insufficient for achieving this alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Layerwise surprisal does not account for layerwise encoding performance, ruling out next-token predictivity as the primary driver.
Intrinsic dimension (Id) peaks in intermediate layers and tracks the construction of higher-order linguistic features (semantic abstraction).
Layerwise Id strongly correlates with layerwise brain encoding performance across models and imaging modalities.
Id and encoding performance grow in tandem over model pre-training, indicating the relationship emerges from learning.
Finetuning models to better predict brain activity causally increases both the Id and semantic content of their representations.
papers.limitation:
High intrinsic dimension is necessary but not sufficient for high neural predictivity, as demonstrated by random Fourier features.
The relationship between Id and encoding performance is weaker for some speech models (e.g., WavLM-base-plus) where low-level acoustic similarity may dominate.
future_direction: Developing better methods for extracting task-relevant structure from naturalistic data to advance encoding models.
Further investigation of linear dimensionality measures in relation to abstraction and encoding performance.
papers.abstract: Research has repeatedly demonstrated that intermediate hidden states extracted from large language models and speech audio models predict measured brain response to natural language stimuli. Yet, very little is known about the representation properties that enable this high prediction performance. Why is it the intermediate layers, and not the output layers, that are most effective for this unique and highly general transfer task? We give evidence that the correspondence between speech and language models and the brain derives from shared meaning abstraction and not their next-word prediction properties. In particular, models construct higher-order linguistic features in their middle layers, cued by a peak in the layerwise intrinsic dimension, a measure of feature complexity. We show that a layer's intrinsic dimension strongly predicts how well it explains fMRI and ECoG signals; that the relation between intrinsic dimension and brain predictivity arises over model pre-training; and finetuning models to better predict the brain causally increases both representations' intrinsic dimension and their semantic content. Results suggest that semantic richness, high intrinsic dimension, and brain predictivity mirror each other, and that the key driver of model-brain similarity is rich meaning abstraction of the inputs, where language modeling is a task sufficiently complex (but perhaps not the only) to require it.

papers.title: Wave to Syntax: Probing spoken language models for syntax
papers.research_question: Do spoken language models encode syntactic structure, and how does it vary across layers, model sizes, and training objectives?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that spoken language models encode syntactic structure, with encoding strongest in middle layers and enhanced by model size and specific training objectives.
papers.conclusion: The results confirm that spoken language models encode a moderate level of syntactic information, with encoding affected by training objectives and model size.
papers.key_findings:
Syntax is encoded in spoken language models, but weaker than in text-based models like BERT.
Syntax encoding is most prominent in the middle layers of the networks.
Larger model size is associated with stronger encoding of syntactic information.
Fine-tuning for ASR improves syntax encoding compared to pre-training only.
Self-supervised objectives lead to a dip in syntax encoding in final layers, while visually-supervised objectives do not.
papers.limitation:
The study only looks at sentence-level representations.
Only English datasets are used.
future_direction: Extend experiments to sub-sentence level probing
Compare syntax encoding across different languages
papers.abstract: Understanding which information is encoded in deep models of spoken and written language has been the focus of much research in recent years, as it is crucial for debugging and improving these architectures. Most previous work has focused on probing for speaker characteristics, acoustic and phonological information in models of spoken language, and for syntactic information in models of written language. Here we focus on the encoding of syntax in several self-supervised and visually grounded models of spoken language. We employ two complementary probing methods, combined with baselines and reference representations to quantify the degree to which syntactic structure is encoded in the activations of the target models. We show that syntax is captured most prominently in the middle layers of the networks, and more explicitly within models with more parameters.

papers.title: Human-like Linguistic Biases in Neural Speech Models: Phonetic Categorization and Phonotactic Constraints in Wav2Vec2.0
papers.research_question: Does the Wav2Vec2 model exhibit human-like biases in phonetic categorization based on phonotactic constraints, and where in the model does this bias emerge?
papers.core_contribution: Wav2Vec2 models exhibit human-like phonotactic biases in phonetic categorization, with the bias emerging in early Transformer layers and being amplified by ASR finetuning but present in self-supervised models.
papers.conclusion: Controlled phonetic categorization experiments can localize linguistic knowledge in neural speech models, revealing human-like phonotactic biases.
papers.key_findings:
Wav2Vec2 models show clear perceptual boundaries in phonetic categorization similar to humans.
The models bias towards phonotactically admissible categories in ambiguous contexts.
This bias emerges around the 4th Transformer layer in finetuned models and is also present in pretrained models.
The bias is absent in untrained and non-speech acoustic models.
Embedding similarities, probing, and CTC-lens provide complementary insights into model internals.
papers.limitation: The study is exploratory and limited to specific phonotactic contexts; more experiments are needed for general conclusions.
future_direction: Study a greater variety of phonological contexts to generalize findings.
Examine more abstract biases like lexical and syntactic contexts.
Investigate robustness across different model architectures.
papers.abstract:
What do deep neural speech models know about phonology? Existing work has
examined the encoding of individual linguistic units such as phonemes in these
models. Here we investigate interactions between units. Inspired by classic
experiments on human speech perception, we study how Wav2Vec2 resolves
phonotactic constraints. We synthesize sounds on an acoustic continuum between
/l/ and /r/ and embed them in controlled contexts where only /l/, only /r/, or
neither occur in English. Like humans, Wav2Vec2 models show a bias towards the
phonotactically admissable category in processing such ambiguous sounds. Using
simple measures to analyze model internals on the level of individual stimuli,
we find that this bias emerges in early layers of the model's Transformer
module. This effect is amplified by ASR finetuning but also present in fully
self-supervised models. Our approach demonstrates how controlled stimulus
designs can help localize specific linguistic knowledge in neural speech
models.

papers.title: Inferring the nature of linguistic computations in the brain
papers.research_question: How can we infer the nature of linguistic computations from neural data, and what are the pitfalls in interpreting such data and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that neural data alone is insufficient to infer the computational mechanisms of sentence processing, and that models must be evaluated based on cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles to be explanatory.
papers.conclusion: Computational modeling is vital for understanding sentence processing, but models must compute linguistically-sufficient representations via explicit cognitive operations and stay faithful to neurophysiological principles, and should not be judged solely on predictive power.
papers.key_findings:
The presence of a 1-2-4 Hz pattern in neural data does not necessarily imply hierarchical processing; it can also arise from associative models.
Artificial neural networks can produce the 1-2-4 Hz pattern without explicit sentence structure, but this does not rule out hierarchical processing in the brain.
Predictive power of a model is not the sole criterion for explaining brain function; models must also be faithful to cognitive and neural principles.
The amount of training data used in ANNs may not reflect the brain's learning environment, and rule-based models might be more explanatory in some cases.
Statistical models are not necessarily more parsimonious than hierarchical models, as they may require extensive training and latent syntactic information.
future_direction: Using naturalistic paradigms to study language processing
Integrating multiple data sources (e.g., EEG, fMRI) to test models
Developing models that are explicit about cognitive operations and neurophysiological implementation
papers.abstract: Sentences contain structure that determines their meaning beyond that of individual words. An influential study by Ding and colleagues (2016) used frequency tagging of phrases and sentences to show that the human brain is sensitive to structure by finding peaks of neural power at the rate at which structures were presented. Since then, there has been a rich debate on how to best explain this pattern of results with profound impact on the language sciences. Models that use hierarchical structure building, as well as models based on associative sequence processing, can predict the neural response, creating an inferential impasse as to which class of models explains the nature of the linguistic computations reflected in the neural readout. In the current manuscript, we discuss pitfalls and common fallacies seen in the conclusions drawn in the literature illustrated by various simulations. We conclude that inferring the neural operations of sentence processing based on these neural data, and any like it, alone, is insufficient. We discuss how to best evaluate models and how to approach the modeling of neural readouts to sentence processing in a manner that remains faithful to cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles.

papers.title: Comparison of Structural Parsers and Neural Language Models as Surprisal Estimators
papers.research_question: How do structural parsers and neural language models compare as surprisal estimators for predicting human sentence processing difficulty?
papers.core_contribution: The proposed structural parser, which incorporates strong linguistic generalizations, achieves comparable or superior fits to human reading times compared to neural language models trained on much more data. Among GPT-2 models, smaller models with fewer parameters fit human data better when training data is held constant.
papers.conclusion: Incremental parsers that embody strong linguistic generalizations are more appropriate as computational-level models of human sentence processing than deep neural language models, which require orders of magnitude more training data and do not provide a better fit to human reading behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Surprisal estimates from the structural parser deliver comparable and often superior fits to self-paced reading and eye-tracking data compared to neural language models.
Among GPT-2 models sharing the same architecture and training data, there is a negative correlation between parameter count and fit to self-paced reading and eye-tracking data.
The character-based morphological word model in the structural parser makes a large contribution to regression model fit, suggesting a role for subword information in sentence processing.
Surprisal estimates from the structural parser and 5-gram model did not contribute as much to fMRI data model fit compared to neural LMs, suggesting different measures are sensitive to different aspects of processing difficulty.
The relationship between language model perplexity and psychometric predictive power is influenced by primary architecture and training data amount, not just model capacity.
future_direction: Future work should continue to focus on incorporating relevant linguistic generalizations into concrete models and evaluating their predictions on human subject data.
papers.abstract: Expectation-based theories of sentence processing posit that processing difficulty is determined by predictability in context. While predictability quantified via surprisal has gained empirical support, this representation-agnostic measure leaves open the question of how to best approximate the human comprehender's latent probability model. This article first describes an incremental left-corner parser that incorporates information about common linguistic abstractions such as syntactic categories, predicate-argument structure, and morphological rules as a computational-level model of sentence processing. The article then evaluates a variety of structural parsers and deep neural language models as cognitive models of sentence processing by comparing the predictive power of their surprisal estimates on self-paced reading, eye-tracking, and fMRI data collected during real-time language processing. The results show that surprisal estimates from the proposed left-corner processing model deliver comparable and often superior fits to self-paced reading and eye-tracking data when compared to those from neural language models trained on much more data. This may suggest that the strong linguistic generalizations made by the proposed processing model may help predict humanlike processing costs that manifest in latency-based measures, even when the amount of training data is limited. Additionally, experiments using Transformer-based language models sharing the same primary architecture and training data show a surprising negative correlation between parameter count and fit to self-paced reading and eye-tracking data. These findings suggest that large-scale neural language models are making weaker generalizations based on patterns of lexical items rather than stronger, more humanlike generalizations based on linguistic structure.

papers.title: Mitigating Negative Interference in Multilingual Knowledge Editing through Null-Space Constraints
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently update knowledge in multilingual large language models sequentially across languages without causing negative interference and while preserving multilingual generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LangEdit, a null-space constrained framework for multilingual sequential knowledge editing that projects parameter updates for each language onto the orthogonal complement of previous updated subspaces, mitigating negative interference and preserving multilingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: LangEdit is an effective framework for multilingual sequential knowledge editing that uses null-space projection to isolate language-specific updates, mitigating negative interference and preserving multilingual generalization, as demonstrated across multiple models and languages.
papers.key_findings:
LangEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance in multilingual sequential knowledge editing, improving editing accuracy and multilingual generalization across three model architectures and six languages.
LangEdit effectively mitigates negative interference by projecting language-specific updates onto the null space of previous updates, preserving performance in previously edited languages.
The method demonstrates cross-lingual knowledge transfer, where edits in one language can be accessed in another without explicit editing in that language.
Editing effectiveness varies by language, with languages having less pretraining data (e.g., Spanish) showing greater improvement than high-resource languages (e.g., English).
LangEdit maintains high specificity, ensuring that edits do not affect unrelated knowledge, and improves downstream task performance on multilingual benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted on 6-8B parameter LLMs; extending to larger architectures (e.g., 70B-scale models) could reveal scaling effects.
The current evaluation focuses on constrained editing scenarios; future work should explore a broader range of downstream applications to assess real-world deployment viability.
Multilingual experiments are limited to 6 languages; developing comprehensive multilingual benchmarks covering hundreds of languages would better test the boundaries of LangEdit and baselines.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger architectures (e.g., 70B-scale models) to reveal scaling effects.
Exploring a broader range of downstream applications to assess real-world deployment viability.
Developing comprehensive multilingual benchmarks covering hundreds of languages.
papers.abstract: Efficiently updating multilingual knowledge in large language models (LLMs), while preserving consistent factual representations across languages, remains a long-standing and unresolved challenge.While deploying separate editing systems for each language might seem viable, this approach incurs substantial costs due to the need to manage multiple models.A more efficient solution involves integrating knowledge updates across all languages into a unified model.However, performing sequential edits across languages often leads to destructive parameter interference, significantly degrading multilingual generalization and the accuracy of injected knowledge.To address this challenge, we propose LangEdit, a novel null-space constrained framework designed to precisely isolate language-specific knowledge updates.The core innovation of LangEdit lies in its ability to project parameter updates for each language onto the orthogonal complement of previous updated subspaces.This approach mathematically guarantees update independence while preserving multilingual generalization capabilities.We conduct a comprehensive evaluation across three model architectures, six languages, and four downstream tasks, demonstrating that LangEdit effectively mitigates parameter interference and outperforms existing state-of-the-art editing methods.Our results highlight its potential for enabling efficient and accurate multilingual knowledge updates in LLMs.The code is available at https: //github.com/VRCMF/LangEdit.git.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models represent different linguistic phenomena, and are linguistically similar phenomena represented similarly in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method using linguistic minimal pairs to measure linguistic similarity in LLMs, revealing that linguistic similarity is influenced by training data, aligns with fine-grained linguistic categories, weakly correlates with semantic similarity, and shows limited cross-lingual alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides insights into LLMs' internal language processing, bridging neural models and linguistic theory, and offers a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages.
Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones.
Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, indicating its context-dependent nature.
LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Dependent on the quality and scope of existing linguistic minimal pair datasets
Limited to three languages, not representing global linguistic diversity
Only captures a fraction of language's complexity with 150 phenomena
future_direction: Developing more high-quality minimal pairs
Broadening language coverage to include more diverse linguistic families
Increasing the range of phenomena studied
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel analysis that leverages linguistic minimal pairs to probe the internal linguistic representations of Large Language Models (LLMs). By measuring the similarity between LLM activation differences across minimal pairs, we quantify the and gain insight into the linguistic knowledge captured by LLMs. Our large-scale experiments, spanning 100+ LLMs and 150k minimal pairs in three languages, reveal properties of linguistic similarity from four key aspects: consistency across LLMs, relation to theoretical categorizations, dependency to semantic context, and cross-lingual alignment of relevant phenomena. Our findings suggest that 1) linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages. 2) Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones. 3) Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, showing its context-dependent nature. 4) LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena. This work demonstrates the potential of minimal pairs as a window into the neural representations of language in LLMs, shedding light on the relationship between LLMs and linguistic theory. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/ChenDelong1999/Linguistic-Similarity

papers.title: Decoding Probing: Revealing Internal Linguistic Structures in Neural Language Models using Minimal Pairs
papers.research_question: How do neural language models capture linguistic information internally, specifically using minimal pairs to probe grammaticality across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel 'decoding probing' method inspired by cognitive neuroscience to reveal internal linguistic structures in neural language models using minimal pairs, demonstrating that self-supervised models capture abstract linguistic features in intermediate layers with distinct patterns for syntax, morphology, and semantics.
papers.conclusion: Decoding probing bridges cognitive neuroscience and NLP, providing insights into hierarchical linguistic feature capture in LMs, with semantics-syntax interface and morphology being more challenging than syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn.
Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and distributed in later layers; more layers are required for complex sentences.
Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax.
