Focusing on the Llama-2 family of transformer models, our study uses carefully constructed non-English prompts with a unique correct single-token continuation. From layer to layer, transformers gradually map an input embedding of the final prompt token to an output embedding from which next-token probabilities are computed. Tracking intermediate embeddings through their high-dimensional space reveals three distinct phases, whereby intermediate embeddings (1) start far away from output token embeddings; (2) already allow for decoding a semantically correct next token in the middle layers, but give higher probability to its version in English than in the input language; (3) finally move into an input-language-specific region of the embedding space. We cast these results into a conceptual model where the three phases operate in "input space", "concept space", and "output space", respectively. Crucially, our evidence suggests that the abstract "concept space" lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding the biases held by multilingual language models.

papers.title: Encoding of lexical tone in self-supervised models of spoken language
papers.research_question: To what extent do self-supervised spoken language models (SLMs) encode lexical tone information in their internal representations, and how does this compare to human perceptual patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Self-supervised spoken language models encode lexical tone significantly even when trained on non-tonal languages, and their perceptual patterns resemble human listeners, but they do not follow the same developmental trajectory as children.
papers.conclusion: SLMs trained on both tonal and non-tonal languages encode tonal information significantly. Fine-tuning for ASR improves tone encoding for tonal language models but harms it for non-tonal ones. SLMs exhibit human-like perceptual patterns but not human-like developmental trajectories.
papers.key_findings:
SLMs encode lexical tone to a significant degree regardless of whether they are trained on tonal or non-tonal languages.
Fine-tuning for ASR enhances tone encoding for models trained on tonal languages but reduces it for models trained on non-tonal languages.
SLMs show patterns similar to human listeners in discriminating Mandarin tone pairs (T2-T3 and T1-T4) and consonant groups.
SLMs do not follow the same developmental trajectory as children, who show earlier sensitivity to tone than to consonant distinctions.
For Vietnamese tones, the Cantonese model performs better than the English model, while the Mandarin model patterns similarly to the English model, possibly due to different acoustic cues.
papers.limitation:
Variation in the size and quality (noisy vs. clean) of training data across the selected models.
Scarce availability of high-quality speech data for underrepresented tonal languages, limiting model availability.
The Vietnamese model was trained on a significantly larger amount of data (13k hours) than others (~1k hours), potentially confounding results.
The Cantonese model uses a different architecture (wav2vec2-conformer) compared to the other wav2vec2-base models.
Test data consists of read speech datasets, which do not reflect the full linguistic diversity of accents and dialects in Mandarin and Vietnamese.
future_direction: Study the encoding of other suprasegmental features such as stress patterns and intonation.
Investigate whether multilingual SLMs encode segmental and suprasegmental features from different languages more robustly.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research has shown that self-supervised Spoken Language Models (SLMs) encode a wide variety of features in human speech from the acoustic, phonetic, phonological, syntactic and semantic levels, to speaker characteristics. The bulk of prior research on representations of phonology has focused on segmental features such as phonemes; the encoding of suprasegmental phonology (such as tone and stress patterns) in SLMs is not yet well understood. Tone is a suprasegmental feature that is present in more than half of the world's languages. This paper aims to analyze the tone encoding capabilities of SLMs, using Mandarin and Vietnamese as case studies. We show that SLMs encode lexical tone to a significant degree even when they are trained on data from non-tonal languages. We further find that SLMs behave similarly to native and non-native human participants in tone and consonant perception studies, but they do not follow the same developmental trajectory.

papers.title: Prosodic Representations of Prominence Classification Neural Networks and Autoencoders Using Bottleneck Features
papers.research_question: What acoustic prosodic representations do binary prominence classification neural networks and autoencoders learn for prominence?
papers.core_contribution: The prosodic representations obtained from bottleneck features and higher-dimensional non-bottleneck features provide good separation of prominence categories, with F0 providing the best overall separation.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn prosodic representations that separate prominence categories, with F0 being the most important feature, and autoencoders preserve this separation along with other acoustic aspects.
papers.key_findings:
The best individual feature for prominence classification was F0, and the best feature combination was energy, F0, and spectral tilt together.
The classification network's hidden layers became increasingly better at discriminating prominence, while early layers captured gender and speaker information.
The autoencoder could separate prominence categories and also discriminate gender and speaker information, with F0 being the best feature.
PCA of the autoencoder bottleneck features showed much of the acoustic variation was due to speaker idiosyncrasies.
The classification network normalized speaker variance in early layers and focused on prominence classification in later layers.
papers.limitation: The study investigated only three acoustic features over words within a fixed temporal (word) context.
future_direction: Extend experiments with larger datasets.
Include additional features such as Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) and duration.
Investigate the importance of using different underlying linguistic units, such as syllables, and different ways of modeling the temporal context.
papers.abstract: Prominence perception has been known to correlate with a complex interplay of the acoustic features of energy, fundamental frequency, spectral tilt, and duration. The contribution and importance of each of these features in distinguishing between prominent and non-prominent units in speech is not always easy to determine, and more so, the prosodic representations that humans and automatic classifiers learn have been difficult to interpret. This work focuses on examining the acoustic prosodic representations that binary prominence classification neural networks and autoencoders learn for prominence. We investigate the complex features learned at different layers of the network as well as the 10-dimensional bottleneck features (BNFs), for the standard acoustic prosodic correlates of prominence separately and in combination. We analyze and visualize the BNFs obtained from the prominence classification neural networks as well as their network activations. The experiments are conducted on a corpus of Dutch continuous speech with manually annotated prominence labels. Our results show that the prosodic representations obtained from the BNFs and higher-dimensional non-BNFs provide good separation of the two prominence categories, with, however, different partitioning of the BNF space for the distinct features, and the best overall separation obtained for F0.

papers.title: A layer-wise analysis of Mandarin and English suprasegmentals in SSL speech models
papers.research_question: How do self-supervised speech models represent suprasegmental categories like Mandarin lexical tone, English lexical stress, and English phrasal accents?
papers.core_contribution: This study shows that SSL speech models learn abstract representations of suprasegmental categories, with best performance in middle layers, language-specificity driven by context networks, and improvements from ASR fine-tuning for lexical features.
papers.conclusion: SSL models of speech learn representations of abstract suprasegmental categories, with performance differences based on pre-training language arising only in the context network, and fine-tuning for ASR improves representations especially for lexical categories.
papers.key_findings:
wav2vec 2.0 learns representations of suprasegmental categories that are strongest in the middle third of the network.
Models are better at representing features that exist in the language of their training data, and this difference is driven by enriched context in transformer blocks, not local acoustic representation.
Fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 improves performance in later layers compared to pre-trained models mainly for lexically contrastive features like tone and stress.
HuBERT and WavLM learn similar representations to wav2vec 2.0, differing mainly in later layer performance.
Representations of suprasegmental categories are abstract and not directly tied to simple acoustic features like F0.
papers.limitation:
L1-penalty reduced convergence issues but did not entirely eliminate them, especially for fine-tuned models on the tone task.
Data limitations in comparability between Switchboard (conversational speech) and GTMC (read speech) create confounds.
future_direction: Conditioning out earlier layer representations to improve reliability of results.
Controlling for lexical identity in the experiment setup.
papers.abstract: This study asks how self-supervised speech models represent suprasegmental categories like Mandarin lexical tone, English lexical stress, and English phrasal accents. Through a series of probing tasks, we make layer-wise comparisons of English and Mandarin 12 layer monolingual models. Our findings suggest that 1) English and Mandarin wav2vec 2.0 models learn contextual representations of abstract suprasegmental categories which are strongest in the middle third of the network. 2) Models are better at representing features that exist in the language of their training data, and this difference is driven by enriched context in transformer blocks, not local acoustic representation. 3) Fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 improves performance in later layers compared to pre-trained models mainly for lexically contrastive features like tone and stress, 4) HuBERT and WavLM learn similar representations to wav2vec 2.0, differing mainly in later layer performance. Our results extend previous understanding of how models represent suprasegmentals and offer new insights into the language-specificity and contextual nature of these representations.

papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: Focusing on Language: Revealing and Exploiting Language Attention Heads in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the role of multi-head self-attention in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs? Specifically, are there language-specific and language-general attention heads, and how can they be used to control model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LAHIS, a method to identify language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs, and shows how modulating these heads can control cross-lingual attention and improve multilingual performance with minimal parameters.
papers.conclusion: The work enhances interpretability of multilingual behaviors in LLMs from the perspective of MHA and presents practical approaches to strengthen multilingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
LAHIS reveals the existence of language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs.
Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer, allowing steering of model attention to target languages.
Modulating language-specific heads mitigates off-target language generation by suppressing English-heads.
A lightweight adaptation using a trainable matrix on language-specific heads improves multilingual question answering accuracy with only 14-20 parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support multilingual understanding and generation. Meanwhile, efforts to interpret their internal mechanisms have emerged, offering insights to enhance multilingual performance. While multi-head self-attention (MHA) has proven critical in many areas, its role in multilingual capabilities remains underexplored. In this work, we study the contribution of MHA in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs. We propose Language Attention Head Importance Scores (LAHIS), an effective and efficient method that identifies attention head importance for multilingual capabilities via a single forward and backward pass through the LLM. Applying LAHIS to Aya-23-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Mistral-7B-v0.1, we reveal the existence of both language-specific and language-general heads. Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer to guide the model toward target language contexts and mitigate off-target language generation issue, contributing to addressing challenges in multilingual LLMs. We also introduce a lightweight adaptation that learns a soft head mask to modulate attention outputs over language heads, requiring only 20 tunable parameters to improve XQuAD accuracy. Overall, our work enhances both the interpretability and multilingual capabilities of LLMs from the perspective of MHA.

papers.title: Analyzing analytical methods: The case of phonology in neural models of spoken language
papers.research_question: How do diagnostic classifiers and representational similarity analysis compare in analyzing neural representations of phonology, and how do factors like learning (trained vs random) and temporal scope (local vs global) affect the outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reporting analysis results with randomly initialized models is crucial, and that global-scope methods tend to yield more consistent results, recommending their use as a complement to local-scope diagnostic methods.
papers.conclusion: The study recommends using global methods as a complement to local diagnostic methods and always including randomly initialized models as a baseline in representational analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Local RSA shows low correlations and does not separate trained vs random models well.
Global methods (both diagnostic and RSA) are more sensitive to learning and show consistent results across layers.
Randomly initialized RNNs encode phoneme information in higher layers due to recurrent connectivity, while random Transformers do not.
The impact of learning is more salient with global representations than local ones.
Attention-based pooling is more erratic and harder to optimize than mean pooling.
papers.limitation: It is difficult to completely control for the many factors of variation in target models due to architectural modifications required by different objectives and datasets.
future_direction: Sample target models with a larger number of plausible combinations of factors.
Further disentangle differences between analytical methods.
papers.abstract: Given the fast development of analysis techniques for NLP and speech processing systems, few systematic studies have been conducted to compare the strengths and weaknesses of each method. As a step in this direction we study the case of representations of phonology in neural network models of spoken language. We use two commonly applied analytical techniques, diagnostic classifiers and representational similarity analysis, to quantify to what extent neural activation patterns encode phonemes and phoneme sequences. We manipulate two factors that can affect the outcome of analysis. First, we investigate the role of learning by comparing neural activations extracted from trained versus randomly-initialized models. Second, we examine the temporal scope of the activations by probing both local activations corresponding to a few milliseconds of the speech signal, and global activations pooled over the whole utterance. We conclude that reporting analysis results with randomly initialized models is crucial, and that global-scope methods tend to yield more consistent results and we recommend their use as a complement to local-scope diagnostic methods.

papers.title: The Geometry of Multilingual Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, facilitating feature extraction for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual language models encode features along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, enabling targeted extraction of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, as shown by causal effects on language modeling performance and direct subspace comparisons.
Subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that encode information such as token vocabularies, and shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages.
Stable language-neutral axes encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech, and these axes are orthogonal to language-sensitive axes.
The identified axes (both language-sensitive and language-neutral) are relatively stable across middle layers of the model.
Token position information is encoded along nonlinear structures like spirals, toruses, and curves in the representation space.
future_direction: Investigate how nonlinear structures (e.g., spirals, toruses) arise from and interact with the dot product self-attention mechanism in Transformer models.
Conduct a more detailed analysis of how specific representational structures are retained across layers.

Assess how multilingual language models encode more complex linguistic features geometrically, and the extent to which representation spaces can be fully decomposed into orthogonal subspaces encoding different features.
papers.abstract: We assess how multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language. Using XLM-R as a case study, we show that languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, evaluated based on causal effects on language modeling performance and direct comparisons between subspaces for 88 languages. The subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that are relatively stable throughout middle layers, and these axes encode information such as token vocabularies. Shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages. However, we also identify stable language-neutral axes that encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech. We visualize representations projected onto language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, identifying language family and part-of-speech clusters, along with spirals, toruses, and curves representing token position information. These results demonstrate that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, allowing the models to extract a variety of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Encoding of phonology in a recurrent neural model of grounded speech
papers.research_question: How is phonological information encoded in the layers of a recurrent neural network model of grounded speech, and how does the encoding change across layers with respect to form and meaning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how phoneme representations are encoded across layers of a recurrent neural network model of grounded speech, finding that phonological information is strongest in lower layers but persists in higher layers, and that the attention mechanism attenuates phonology to achieve semantic invariance.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that phonological information is encoded most strongly in lower layers of the model, but persists in higher layers, and that the attention mechanism filters out phonological details to focus on semantic meaning.
papers.key_findings:
Phoneme representations are most salient in the lower layers of the model, where low-level signals are processed at a fine-grained level.
A large amount of phonological information is retained at the top recurrent layer.
The attention mechanism following the top recurrent layer significantly attenuates encoding of phonology and makes utterance embeddings more invariant to synonymy.
Hierarchical clustering of phoneme representations learned by the network shows an organizational structure similar to linguistic classifications.
The model can discriminate phonemes with high accuracy, and lower layers are more informative for this task than higher layers or input features.
papers.limitation: The model is trained on synthetic speech, which is easier to process than natural human-generated speech.
future_direction: Apply the methodology to grounded human speech to investigate whether context and speaker-invariant phoneme representations can be learned from natural, noisy input.
Compare the results to similar analyses applied to neuroimaging data.
papers.abstract: We study the representation and encoding of phonemes in a recurrent neural network model of grounded speech. We use a model which processes images and their spoken descriptions, and projects the visual and auditory representations into the same semantic space. We perform a number of analyses on how information about individual phonemes is encoded in the MFCC features extracted from the speech signal, and the activations of the layers of the model. Via experiments with phoneme decoding and phoneme discrimination we show that phoneme representations are most salient in the lower layers of the model, where low-level signals are processed at a fine-grained level, although a large amount of phonological information is retain at the top recurrent layer. We further find out that the attention mechanism following the top recurrent layer significantly attenuates encoding of phonology and makes the utterance embeddings much more invariant to synonymy. Moreover, a hierarchical clustering of phoneme representations learned by the network shows an organizational structure of phonemes similar to those proposed in linguistics.

papers.title: What Language(s) Does Aya-23 Think In? How Multilinguality Affects Internal Language Representations
papers.research_question: How does balanced multilingual training affect internal language processing in LLMs, specifically in terms of language activation, neuron sharing, and layer-wise distribution of language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Balanced multilingual training leads to distinct internal language processing, with language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of typologically related languages during translation, unlike English-centric models.
papers.conclusion: Balanced multilingual training fundamentally alters how decoder-only LLMs process language internally, leading to language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of multiple languages during translation.
papers.key_findings:
Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language.
Code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one.
Aya-23’s language-specific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models.
Neuron overlap analysis shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types.
French-based code-mixed inputs show higher neuron clustering than Chinese-based inputs across all models, regardless of training data composition.
papers.limitation:
Token overlap between languages in the logit lens experiments may affect analysis of language-specific activation patterns.
Neuron specialization analysis using binary activations results in information loss that may obscure subtle activation patterns.
Code-mixed dataset created via rule-based word-to-word translation produces unnatural sentences that may not represent authentic code-switching.
Analysis is limited to three models and may not generalize to other architectures or sizes.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multilingual tasks, yet their internal language processing remains poorly understood. We analyze how Aya-23-8B, a decoder-only LLM trained on balanced multilingual data, handles code-mixed, cloze, and translation tasks compared to predominantly monolingual models like Llama 3 and Chinese-LLaMA-2. Using logit lens and neuron specialization analyses, we find: (1) Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language; (2) code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one; and (3) Aya-23's languagespecific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models. Neuron overlap analysis further shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types. These findings reveal how multilingual training shapes LLM internals and inform future cross-lingual transfer research.

papers.title: [b]=[d]-[t]+[p]: Self-supervised Speech Models Discover Phonological Vector Arithmetic
papers.research_question: Do self-supervised speech models (S3Ms) represent phonology in an analogous compositional manner?
papers.core_contribution: Self-supervised speech models encode phonological features as linear directions in their representation space, and the scale of these phonological vectors corresponds to the degree of acoustic realization of the features.
papers.conclusion: S3Ms encode speech using phonologically interpretable and compositional vectors, demonstrating phonological vector arithmetic.
papers.key_findings:
S3M representations exhibit phonological vector arithmetic, meaning there exist linear directions corresponding to phonological features.
The scale of phonological vectors correlates with acoustic measurements, allowing continuous control of speech synthesis.
S3Ms generalize phonological analogies to unseen phones and languages.
Vowels and consonants show different layerwise trends in success rates, suggesting different contextualization needs.
Phonological vectors are not binary but continuous, enabling fine-grained control over acoustic variation.
papers.abstract: Self-supervised speech models (S3Ms) are known to encode rich phonetic information, yet how this information is structured remains underexplored. We conduct a comprehensive study across 96 languages to analyze the underlying structure of S3M representations, with particular attention to phonological vectors. We first show that there exist linear directions within the model's representation space that correspond to phonological features. We further demonstrate that the scale of these phonological vectors correlate to the degree of acoustic realization of their corresponding phonological features in a continuous manner. For example, the difference between [d] and [t] yields a voicing vector: adding this vector to [p] produces [b], while scaling it results in a continuum of voicing. Together, these findings indicate that S3Ms encode speech using phonologically interpretable and compositional vectors, demonstrating phonological vector arithmetic. All code and interactive demos are available at https://github.com/juice500ml/phonetic-arithmetic .

papers.title: Tracing Multilingual Representations in LLMs with Cross-Layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs form shared representations across languages with language-specific decoding, and why does performance favor the dominant training language such as English?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs form a shared language-agnostic representation space in middle layers, with language-specific decoding in late layers; performance gaps are mechanistically explained by tokenizer bias and feature strength differences.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs use shared representations in middle layers and language-specific decoding in late layers, with performance gaps explained by feature strength and tokenizer bias.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs consistently form a shared language-agnostic space in middle layers, regardless of English dominance in training data.
Language-specific decoding depends on a small set of high-frequency features in late layers that linearly encode language identity from early layers.
Non-English performance failures are linked to dim late-layer features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer bias forcing early layers to specialize in word reassembly.
Finetuning strengthens these features and their connections, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding.
The shared multilingual space emerges as an architectural property, even when models are trained without English.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) can process many languages, yet how they internally represent this diversity remains unclear. Do they form shared multilingual representations with language-specific decoding, and if so, why does performance favor the dominant training language? To address this, we train models on different multilingual mixtures and analyze their internal mechanisms using Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) and Attribution Graphs. Our results reveal multilingual shared representations: the model employs highly similar features across languages, while language-specific decoding emerges in later layers. Training models without English shows identical multilingual shared space structures. Decoding relies partly on a small set of high-frequency features in the final layers, which linearly encode language identity from early layers. Intervening on these features allows one language to be suppressed and another substituted. Finally, to explain non-English failures, we perform a Model-Diffing experiment: underperformance arises from dim late-layer features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer bias toward English that forces early layers to specialize in word reassembly. Finetuning strengthens these features and their links, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding, providing a mechanistic explanation for multilingual gaps. Our models and CLTs are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/CausalNLP/multilingual-clts and https://huggingface.co/collections/CausalNLP/multilingual-gpt2-models. Our code is available at: https://github.com/abirharrasse/MultilingualCLTs

papers.title: A Joint Matrix Factorization Analysis of Multilingual Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models encode morphosyntactic features in their layers? Are the findings robust in low-resource settings? Do morphosyntactic typology and downstream task performance reflect in the factorization outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a joint matrix factorization tool for analyzing multilingual representations and finds that morphosyntactic encoding varies across layers, influenced by language properties, and the tool's outputs correlate with phylogenetic trees and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The joint matrix factorization tool provides insights into multilingual representations, showing layer-wise variations in morphosyntactic encoding and correlations with linguistic properties and task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding of morphosyntactic information decreases from lower to upper layers in multilingual models.
Language-specific factors like writing system and number of unique characters influence encoding.
Multilingual representations show distinct patterns in languages with low proximity.
Low-resource languages benefit from related languages in the model.
Factorization outputs yield hierarchical clusters resembling phylogenetic trees and predict cross-lingual task performance.
papers.limitation:
Only used RoBERTa and XLM-R models, not other available models like BERT or T5.
Downsampled Wikipedia data for equal representation, which may not reflect full-scale training.
Analysis limited to morphosyntactic features, not other linguistic aspects.
future_direction: Extend analysis tool to examine representations learned by multimodal models.
Expand scope to include other linguistic aspects such as semantics and pragmatics.
papers.abstract: We present an analysis tool based on joint matrix factorization for comparing latent representations of multilingual and monolingual models. An alternative to probing, this tool allows us to analyze multiple sets of representations in a joint manner. Using this tool, we study to what extent and how morphosyntactic features are reflected in the representations learned by multilingual pre-trained models. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of over 33 languages and 17 morphosyntactic categories. Our findings demonstrate variations in the encoding of morphosyntactic information across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties. Hierarchical clustering of the factorization outputs yields a tree structure that is related to phylogenetic trees manually crafted by linguists. Moreover, we find the factorization outputs exhibit strong associations with performance observed across different cross-lingual tasks. We release our code to facilitate future research.

papers.title: From Monolingual to Bilingual: Investigating Language Conditioning in Large Language Models for Psycholinguistic Tasks
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages, and how does language identity (monolingual vs bilingual prompting) affect their output behavior and internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models condition their psycholinguistic behavior and internal representations on the language identity specified in the prompt, with differences between monolingual and bilingual prompting, offering insights into cross-linguistic cognition in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results demonstrate that LLMs are not language-neutral. Instead, they respond to and encode language-specific cues in both their outputs and internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Both models adapt their outputs based on the linguistic identity embedded in the prompt.
Qwen shows greater sensitivity to prompt language and sharper behavioral distinctions between Dutch and Chinese than Llama.
Probing reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more linearly decodable in deeper layers.
Chinese prompts yield stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch prompts.
Bilingual prompting can introduce interference or noise, especially for low-resource languages like Dutch.
papers.limitation:
Focus on only three languages (English, Dutch, Chinese), limiting generalizability.
Only two LLMs are evaluated.
Tasks represent only a narrow slice of the psycholinguistic space.
future_direction: Expanding to include languages with different scripts, phonological systems, or morphological complexity (e.g., Arabic, Hindi, Finnish).
Incorporating a broader set of psycholinguistic phenomena, such as lexical decision making, semantic priming, syntactic ambiguity resolution, and metaphor comprehension.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic capabilities, but little is known about how they encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages. We investigate whether and how LLMs exhibit human-like psycholinguistic responses under different linguistic identities using two tasks: sound symbolism and word valence. We evaluate two models, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, under monolingual and bilingual prompting in English, Dutch, and Chinese. Behaviorally, both models adjust their outputs based on prompted language identity, with Qwen showing greater sensitivity and sharper distinctions between Dutch and Chinese. Probing analysis reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more decodable in deeper layers, with Chinese prompts yielding stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch. Our results demonstrate that language identity conditions both output behavior and internal representations in LLMs, providing new insights into their application as models of cross-linguistic cognition.

papers.title: Models of Visually Grounded Speech Signal Pay Attention to Nouns: A Bilingual Experiment on English and Japanese
papers.research_question: What is the behavior of attention in neural models of visually grounded speech trained on English and Japanese, and does it focus on nouns?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that attention in neural models of visually grounded speech focuses on nouns across English and Japanese, and demonstrates cross-lingual speech retrieval using images as pivots.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that attention in visually grounded speech models focuses on nouns across languages, with language-specific adaptations, and enables cross-lingual retrieval using images as pivots.
papers.key_findings:
Attention primarily focuses on nouns in both English and Japanese models.
The Japanese model also pays attention to particles, developing a language-specific behavior similar to human toddlers.
Attention peaks are located at word endings in English and at both beginnings and endings in Japanese.
Images can be used as pivots for cross-lingual speech-to-speech retrieval without parallel data.
The model exhibits noun-bias, aligning with theories of child language acquisition.
papers.limitation: The study uses synthetic speech with only one voice, whereas prior work used real speech with multiple speakers.
future_direction: Validate the methodology on a bilingual dataset featuring real voices.
Extract a bilingual speech-to-speech dictionary using attention peaks as anchor points.
papers.abstract: We investigate the behaviour of attention in neural models of visually grounded speech trained on two languages: English and Japanese. Experimental results show that attention focuses on nouns and this behaviour holds true for two very typologically different languages. We also draw parallels between artificial neural attention and human attention and show that neural attention focuses on word endings as it has been theorised for human attention. Finally, we investigate how two visually grounded monolingual models can be used to perform cross-lingual speech-to-speech retrieval. For both languages, the enriched bilingual (speech-image) corpora with part-of-speech tags and forced alignments are distributed to the community for reproducible research.

papers.title: What does BERT learn about prosody?
papers.research_question: What prosodic information, specifically regarding prosodic prominence, does BERT capture in its representations during pre-training?
papers.core_contribution: BERT learns prosodic prominence information distributed across layers, with a focus on middle layers, indicating reliance on syntactic and semantic cues.
papers.conclusion: BERT captures information about prosodic prominence through a widespread allocation of weights across its layers, indicating reliance on syntactic and semantic information, with POS features in early layers.
papers.key_findings:
BERT captures prosodic prominence information with weights distributed across multiple layers, peaking at layer 3.
Part-of-speech (POS) information is primarily encoded in the early layers of BERT.
Frozen BERT achieves high accuracy in prominence prediction, comparable to prior work.
Fine-tuning BERT for prominence prediction leads to decreased performance due to overfitting.
The pattern of layer weights for prominence is similar across different datasets, suggesting consistent linguistic reliance.
papers.limitation: Performance differences across datasets may be due to varying speaking styles and prominence coding schemes.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to more datasets.
Incorporate integrated gradients as an attribution method.
Examine differences between read and dialogue speech styles.
papers.abstract: Language models have become nearly ubiquitous in natural language processing applications achieving state-of-the-art results in many tasks including prosody. As the model design does not define predetermined linguistic targets during training but rather aims at learning generalized representations of the language, analyzing and interpreting the representations that models implicitly capture is important in bridging the gap between interpretability and model performance. Several studies have explored the linguistic information that models capture providing some insights on their representational capacity. However, the current studies have not explored whether prosody is part of the structural information of the language that models learn. In this work, we perform a series of experiments on BERT probing the representations captured at different layers. Our results show that information about prosodic prominence spans across many layers but is mostly focused in middle layers suggesting that BERT relies mostly on syntactic and semantic information.

papers.title: Layer by Layer: Uncovering Hidden Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the final layer always yield the best representation for downstream tasks, or can intermediate layers provide better representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that intermediate layers in language models often outperform final layers on downstream tasks, and introduces a unified information-theoretic framework to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that intermediate layers often provide superior representations, challenging the default use of final layers, and provides a framework for understanding representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers across diverse architectures and tasks.
Autoregressive models exhibit a pronounced mid-layer compression valley, while masked or bidirectional models show milder changes.
The effect is domain-general, also observed in autoregressive vision transformers.
Chain-of-thought fine-tuning reshapes mid-layer entropy, preserving latent context for multi-step reasoning.
Intermediate layers strike a balance between information compression and signal preservation.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying causes of intermediate layer compression and do explicit finetuning to control compression.
papers.abstract: From extracting features to generating text, the outputs of large language models (LLMs) typically rely on the final layers, following the conventional wisdom that earlier layers capture only low-level cues. However, our analysis shows that intermediate layers can encode even richer representations, often improving performance on a range of downstream tasks. To explain and quantify these hidden-layer properties, we propose a unified framework of representation quality metrics based on information theory, geometry, and invariance to input perturbations. Our framework highlights how each layer balances information compression and signal preservation, revealing why mid-depth embeddings can exceed the last layer's performance. Through extensive experiments on 32 text-embedding tasks across various architectures (transformers, state-space models) and domains (language, vision), we demonstrate that intermediate layers consistently provide stronger features, challenging the standard view on final-layer embeddings and opening new directions on using mid-layer representations for more robust and accurate representations.

papers.title: Diverging views on the role of structured representations in linguistics and language modeling
papers.research_question: How do language models compare to human language processing in terms of structured representations, and what is their role in the science of language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that language models struggle with structured representations central to human language, and suggests that for language models to be effective models of language, structured representations must be incorporated as computational objects.
papers.conclusion: Language models need to conceptualize structured representations as computational objects to better align with human language and contribute to the science of language.
papers.key_findings:
Language models trained on next-word prediction may not learn structure-dependent representations necessary for human language.
Models like ChatGPT show insensitivity to Binding Principle C, incorrectly allowing co-reference in prohibited contexts.
Language models do not make a qualitative distinction between possible and impossible languages, treating them similarly unlike humans.
The internal representational infrastructure for possible and impossible languages overlaps in models, indicating no fundamental difference.
Incorporating structured representations as primary computational targets could enhance language models' utility as models of language.
future_direction: Incorporate structured representations as computational objects in language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent years have seen dramatic advances in the linguistic abilities of language models, leading some authors to argue that they can be treated as models of language. Against this background, we provide a cognitive perspective on the place of language models in the science of language, with a particular focus on the role of structured representations. Evidence from linguistics, psychology and cognitive neuroscience shows that structured representations occupy a central place in the human mind. Structured representations constrain how linguistic forms map onto meanings, thereby determining the boundaries of possible human languages. In language modeling, instead, the place of structured representations is often peripheral. They are seen as optional end point of modeling, to be induced as a consequence of the objective the model tries to optimize – that is, next-word prediction. Because structured relations and representations are not necessarily useful for predicting the next word in a sequence, it is not guaranteed that the model’s internal organization will come to encode those representations. Indeed, contemporary language models struggle to use structured representations functionally to map form onto meaning, and to determine whether they should consider their input as a possible human language or not. Building on classic insights in linguistics and (computational) cognitive science, we suggest that any use of language models as models of language requires conceptualizing the role of structured representations as computational objects.

papers.title: Emergent morpho-phonological representations in self-supervised speech models
papers.research_question: What types of linguistic representations are necessary for word recognition in self-supervised speech models, and how do they represent phonological and morphological phenomena in English inflections?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that self-supervised speech models optimized for word recognition represent abstract distributional constraints linking English nouns and verbs to their regular inflected forms, rather than separate phonological or morphological units.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that self-supervised speech models optimized for word recognition represent abstract phonological regularities, challenging the presumed necessity of distinct linguistic representations of phonology and morphology in spoken word recognition.
papers.key_findings:
The word probe model exhibits a global linear geometry that can link inflected nouns and verbs to their base forms.
This representation is largely invariant to morphological contrasts between noun plurals and verb inflections.
It is also invariant to phonological contrasts between allomorphs [z], [s], and [Iz].
The representation tracks distributional constraints governing word-final sounds, preferring phonologically consistent forms.
Optimizing for word recognition reduces sensitivity to morphological and phonological details compared to the base Wav2Vec model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on a small set of morphological and phonological phenomena in English.
The linear geometric assumption may yield false positives and false negatives.
future_direction: Extend to other English phenomena with dual patterning of morphology and phonology.
Use multilingual or monolingual non-English models to verify that patterns are generalizations from English phonology.
papers.abstract: Self-supervised speech models can be trained to efficiently recognize spoken words in naturalistic, noisy environments. However, we do not understand the types of linguistic representations these models use to accomplish this task. To address this question, we study how S3M variants optimized for word recognition represent phonological and morphological phenomena in frequent English noun and verb inflections. We find that their representations exhibit a global linear geometry which can be used to link English nouns and verbs to their regular inflected forms. This geometric structure does not directly track phonological or morphological units. Instead, it tracks the regular distributional relationships linking many word pairs in the English lexicon -- often, but not always, due to morphological inflection. These findings point to candidate representational strategies that may support human spoken word recognition, challenging the presumed necessity of distinct linguistic representations of phonology and morphology.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: Probing self-attention in self-supervised speech models for cross-linguistic differences
papers.research_question: What are the cross-linguistic differences in self-attention mechanisms of self-supervised speech models, and do they learn language-independent representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that self-supervised speech models learn diverse attention patterns with cross-linguistic similarities, and diagonal attention heads are most important for phoneme classification.
papers.conclusion: The study finds that diagonal attention heads are essential for phoneme classification in speech models, and pruning strategies based on head importance may be applicable across languages, despite some cross-linguistic differences.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in TERA are diverse, ranging from diagonal to global, regardless of training language.
Turkish-trained models have more vertical heads compared to English-trained models.
Phoneme relation maps show no clear cross-linguistic differences; phonemes primarily attend to themselves.
Diagonal heads are crucial for phoneme classification, and masking them significantly reduces accuracy.
Global and vertical heads can be pruned with less impact, suggesting efficient pruning strategies cross-linguistically.
papers.limitation:
Noisy Turkish data due to alignment issues affects accuracy metrics.
Limited availability of Turkish speech data constrains the study.
Small model size may limit the generalizability of results.
future_direction: Expand attention analysis to more fine-grained categories.
Extend the methodology to other self-supervised transformer models and languages.
Improve data quality and alignment methods for better evaluation.
papers.abstract: Speech models have gained traction thanks to increase in accuracy from novel transformer architectures. While this impressive increase in performance across automatic speech recognition (ASR) benchmarks is noteworthy, there is still much that is unknown about the use of attention mechanisms for speech-related tasks. For example, while it is assumed that these models are learning language-independent (i.e., universal) speech representations, there has not yet been an in-depth exploration of what it would mean for the models to be language-independent. In the current paper, we explore this question within the realm of self-attention mechanisms of one small self-supervised speech transformer model (TERA). We find that even with a small model, the attention heads learned are diverse ranging from almost entirely diagonal to almost entirely global regardless of the training language. We highlight some notable differences in attention patterns between Turkish and English and demonstrate that the models do learn important phonological information during pretraining. We also present a head ablation study which shows that models across languages primarily rely on diagonal heads to classify phonemes.

papers.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphosyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages.
papers.core_contribution: Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.
papers.conclusion: Large language models share representations of morphosyntactic concepts across typologically diverse languages, suggesting that they develop cross-lingual abstractions, even when trained primarily on English.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of morphosyntactic concepts are shared across languages, with significant overlap in the top features encoding grammatical categories.
Probing classifiers crucially rely on multilingual features to predict morphosyntactic concepts; ablating multilingual features drops performance to near-chance.
Intervening on single multilingual features can change model behavior in machine translation tasks, demonstrating their causal role.
Interventions are selective, primarily affecting the targeted concept without interfering with other concepts.
Sparse autoencoder features are human-interpretable and activate on relevant grammatical concepts across languages.
papers.limitation:
Distinction between model understanding and generation; some features with high causal effect on probes do not necessarily affect generation.
Human biases in feature interpretation; human explanations of features may be biased and suboptimal.
Sparse autoencoders only recover linearly encoded features; non-linearly encoded concepts may not be captured.
papers.abstract: Human bilinguals often use similar brain regions to process multiple languages, depending on when they learned their second language and their proficiency. In large language models (LLMs), how are multiple languages learned and encoded? In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphsyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages. We train sparse autoencoders on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, and demonstrate that abstract grammatical concepts are often encoded in feature directions shared across many languages. We use causal interventions to verify the multilingual nature of these representations; specifically, we show that ablating only multilingual features decreases classifier performance to near-chance across languages. We then use these features to precisely modify model behavior in a machine translation task; this demonstrates both the generality and selectivity of these feature's roles in the network. Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Human-Like Internally
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether surprisal (negative log probability) from internal layers of large language models aligns with human sentence processing data, and whether the alignment varies by layer depth and the type of human measure (behavioral vs. neurophysiological).
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that surprisal from internal layers of larger language models aligns well with human sentence processing data, challenging prior conclusions that focused on final layers. Additionally, it finds that earlier layers align with fast human measures (e.g., gaze duration) and later layers with slower measures (e.g., N400).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that larger language models are cognitively plausible when internal layers are considered, and that different layers correspond to different stages of human sentence processing, advocating for layer-wise alignment in cognitive modeling.
papers.key_findings:
Surprisal from internal layers of larger LMs aligns with human sentence processing data as well as or better than smaller LMs.
The last layer does not yield the best alignment; the best layer varies by human measure.
Earlier layers align better with fast human measures (e.g., first-pass gaze duration, self-paced reading time), while later layers align better with slower measures (e.g., N400, MAZE processing time).
When considering the best internal layer, larger LMs show a positive scaling effect (larger models have higher ∆LL) for most human measures.
The alignment patterns are consistent across multiple languages (tested on MECO corpus).
papers.limitation: The study is focused on naturalistic reading corpora and does not include controlled experiments on syntactic ambiguity or grammatical violation, which are known challenges for surprisal theory.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other probability-based measures such as entropy and entropy reduction.
Combine the internal layer approach with linguistically-motivated neural models.
papers.abstract: Recent cognitive modeling studies have reported that larger language models (LMs) exhibit a poorer fit to human reading behavior (Oh and Schuler, 2023b; Shain et al., 2024; Kuribayashi et al., 2024), leading to claims of their cognitive implausibility. In this paper, we revisit this argument through the lens of mechanistic interpretability and argue that prior conclusions were skewed by an exclusive focus on the final layers of LMs. Our analysis reveals that next-word probabilities derived from internal layers of larger LMs align with human sentence processing data as well as, or better than, those from smaller LMs. This alignment holds consistently across behavioral (self-paced reading times, gaze durations, MAZE task processing times) and neurophysiological (N400 brain potentials) measures, challenging earlier mixed results and suggesting that the cognitive plausibility of larger LMs has been underestimated. Furthermore, we first identify an intriguing relationship between LM layers and human measures: earlier layers correspond more closely with fast gaze durations, while later layers better align with relatively slower signals such as N400 potentials and MAZE processing times. Our work opens new avenues for interdisciplinary research at the intersection of mechanistic interpretability and cognitive modeling.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 1, Learning Hierarchical Language Structures
papers.research_question: How do language models perform deep reasoning over hierarchical structures, and can we understand their inner workings using synthetic context-free grammars (CFGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers can learn complex context-free grammars and that their hidden states linearly encode non-terminal information, while attention patterns mimic dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn complex hierarchical structures defined by CFGs, and their internal representations and attention patterns align with dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers (GPT variants) can accurately learn and generate strings from synthetic CFGs that require dynamic programming to parse.
Hidden states of the trained transformers linearly encode non-terminal ancestor information almost perfectly.
Attention patterns in the trained models resemble the information flow of dynamic programming, with boundary-based attention.
Relative and rotary positional embeddings are crucial for learning harder CFGs, outperforming absolute positional embeddings.
Training with perturbed data (10% noise) improves robustness to corrupted prefixes.
papers.limitation: The chosen CFGs are synthetic and may not encompass all CFGs; the results are specific to the designed CFG families.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models are effective but complex, and understanding their inner workings and reasoning mechanisms is a significant challenge. Previous research has primarily explored how these models handle simple tasks like name copying or selection, and we extend this by investigating how these models perform recursive language structure reasoning defined by context-free grammars (CFGs). We introduce a family of synthetic CFGs that produce hierarchical rules, capable of generating lengthy sentences (e.g., hundreds of tokens) that are locally ambiguous and require dynamic programming to parse. Despite this complexity, we demonstrate that generative models like GPT can accurately learn and reason over CFG-defined hierarchies and generate sentences based on it. We explore the model's internals, revealing that its hidden states precisely capture the structure of CFGs, and its attention patterns resemble the information passing in a dynamic programming algorithm. This paper also presents several corollaries, including showing why absolute positional embeddings is inferior to relative and rotary embeddings; uniform attention alone is surprisingly effective (motivating our follow-up work on Canon layers); encoder-only models (e.g., BERT, DeBERTa) struggle with deep structure reasoning on CFGs compared to autoregressive models (e.g., GPT); and injecting structural or syntactic noise into pretraining data markedly improves robustness to corrupted language prompts.

papers.title: Investigating Disentanglement in a Phoneme-level Speech Codec for Prosody Modeling
papers.research_question: How can a phoneme-level discrete neural codec achieve disentanglement of prosodic information from linguistic content and speaker characteristics?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a phoneme-level neural codec that learns disentangled prosodic representations, with interpretable latent space where principal components correspond to pitch and energy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed phoneme-level neural codec successfully learns disentangled prosodic representations, with interpretable and transferable latent codes, enabling effective prosody modeling and control.
papers.key_findings:
Latent codes are disentangled from speaker and linguistic information, as shown by low ASR error rates when codes are shuffled.
Principal components of the latent space correspond to pitch and energy, encoded in a speaker-relative way.
The model enables effective prosody transfer between utterances, with high correlation in F0 and energy.
The discrete bottleneck does not harm modeling capacity, performing similarly to a continuous model on reconstruction metrics.
Cross-resynthesis maintains naturalness and speaker similarity, indicating effective disentanglement.
papers.limitation:
The model relies on pre-calculated phoneme durations from a forced aligner, which may not be optimal.
The latent dimensionality choice may require more detailed study.
future_direction: Train the model on larger datasets with hundreds or thousands of speakers.
Integrate a duration predictor to avoid relying on pre-calculated durations.
Investigate if the latent representation facilitates training effective prior models for TTS or voice conversion.
papers.abstract: Most of the prevalent approaches in speech prosody modeling rely on learning global style representations in a continuous latent space which encode and transfer the attributes of reference speech. However, recent work on neural codecs which are based on Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) already shows great potential offering distinct advantages. We investigate the prosody modeling capabilities of the discrete space of such an RVQ-VAE model, modifying it to operate on the phoneme-level. We condition both the encoder and decoder of the model on linguistic representations and apply a global speaker embedding in order to factor out both phonetic and speaker information. We conduct an extensive set of investigations based on subjective experiments and objective measures to show that the phoneme-level discrete latent representations obtained this way achieves a high degree of disentanglement, capturing fine-grained prosodic information that is robust and transferable. The latent space turns out to have interpretable structure with its principal components corresponding to pitch and energy.

papers.title: Enhancing Multilingual Text Understanding viaTransformer-Based Meta-Learning
papers.research_question: How can multilingual text understanding be enhanced by integrating structured linguistic knowledge (syntactic and semantic) into transformer-based models via meta-learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel framework that synergizes symbolic linguistic formalism with neural representation learning via a Grammar-Infused Representation Alignment (GIRA) strategy, enhancing multilingual text understanding by aligning neural attention mechanisms with syntactic dependencies.
papers.conclusion: The integration of grammatical constraints via GIRA into a transformer-based meta-learning framework significantly improves multilingual text understanding, though limitations exist in handling noisy language and reliance on syntactic annotations.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed model (LexiStruct with GIRA) outperforms baseline methods on multiple multilingual benchmarks (XNLI, MLDoc, TyDiQAt, WikiAnn) across metrics like NDCG, Recall, MRR, and Hit Rate.
Ablation studies show that key components (Syntactic Structure Injection, Syntax-Semantics Alignment, Grammar-Semantics Alignment) are essential for the model's performance, with removal of any leading to significant drops in metrics.
The integration of grammatical constraints via GIRA improves the model's robustness and interpretability in multilingual understanding tasks.
papers.limitation:
The integration of grammatical constraints may reduce the model's flexibility in handling less-structured or noisy language inputs, such as colloquialisms or code-switching phenomena.
