The current implementation assumes access to high-quality syntactic annotations, which may not be available for all languages, especially low-resource ones.
future_direction: Explore strategies for relaxing the assumption of high-quality syntactic annotations, possibly through unsupervised or semi-supervised learning of syntactic structures.
Extend the model's adaptability to more diverse and informal language domains to improve broader applicability in real-world multilingual settings.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> In the evolving landscape of computational sciences, the integration of structured linguistic knowledge into deep learningmodels has become increasingly vital for advancing multilingual text understanding. Traditional transformer-based architectures,while powerful, often lack the capacity to inherently capture the syntactic and semantic nuances present across diverselanguages, leading to limitations in generalization and interpretability. To address these challenges, we introduce a novelframework that synergizes symbolic linguistic formalism with neural representation learning. Our approach employsa structure-aware neural language model that incorporates grammatical constraints directly into the learning process,enhancing the model’s ability to comprehend and process multilingual data effectively. Central to our methodology is theGrammar-Infused Representation Alignment (GIRA) strategy, which aligns neural attention mechanisms with syntacticdependencies, ensuring that the model’s internal representations adhere to linguistic structures. Experimental evaluationsdemonstrate that our model achieves superior performance in multilingual understanding tasks, exhibiting enhanced robustnessinterpretability. This work contributes to the field by offering a principled method that bridges the gap between statistical learningand linguistic theory, aligning with the journal’s commitment to advancing both fundamental and applied computational sciences.

papers.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in Transformers work? The paper hypothesizes that Transformers implement gradient descent in their forward pass to learn from in-context data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers trained on auto-regressive objectives implement gradient descent in their forward pass, providing a mechanistic understanding of in-context learning for regression tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning in Transformers can be understood as gradient descent in the forward pass, at least for regression tasks, providing a mechanistic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
A single linear self-attention layer can be constructed to perform one step of gradient descent on a linear regression loss.
When trained on linear regression tasks, linear self-attention-only Transformers converge to weights that match the gradient descent construction.
Multiple layers of self-attention can implement multiple steps of gradient descent and even surpass plain gradient descent by learning a curvature correction (GD++).
Transformers with MLPs can solve nonlinear regression tasks by learning linear models on deep representations.
The paper connects the induction head mechanism to in-context learning by gradient descent.
papers.limitation:
The findings on linear self-attention-only Transformers only explain a limited part of a complex process, and it may be one of many possible methods giving rise to in-context learning.
The analysis is limited to regression tasks and simple Transformer architectures.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to language modeling and other domains.
Investigating the role of softmax and LayerNorm in in-context learning.
Exploring the connection to hypernetworks and weight generation.
papers.abstract: At present, the mechanisms of in-context learning in Transformers are not well understood and remain mostly an intuition. In this paper, we suggest that training Transformers on auto-regressive objectives is closely related to gradient-based meta-learning formulations. We start by providing a simple weight construction that shows the equivalence of data transformations induced by 1) a single linear self-attention layer and by 2) gradient-descent (GD) on a regression loss. Motivated by that construction, we show empirically that when training self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression tasks either the models learned by GD and Transformers show great similarity or, remarkably, the weights found by optimization match the construction. Thus we show how trained Transformers become mesa-optimizers i.e. learn models by gradient descent in their forward pass. This allows us, at least in the domain of regression problems, to mechanistically understand the inner workings of in-context learning in optimized Transformers. Building on this insight, we furthermore identify how Transformers surpass the performance of plain gradient descent by learning an iterative curvature correction and learn linear models on deep data representations to solve non-linear regression tasks. Finally, we discuss intriguing parallels to a mechanism identified to be crucial for in-context learning termed induction-head (Olsson et al., 2022) and show how it could be understood as a specific case of in-context learning by gradient descent learning within Transformers. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at https://github.com/google-research/self-organising-systems/tree/master/transformers_learn_icl_by_gd .

papers.title: Structural Persistence in Language Models: Priming as a Window into Abstract Language Representations
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether modern neural language models exhibit structural priming, what factors influence the priming effect, and the nature of the structural representations they acquire.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer language models exhibit structural priming, indicating they encode abstract structural information, and that this priming is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, with evidence for hierarchical syntactic representations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that Transformer language models are susceptible to structural priming, revealing they encode abstract structural information that is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, and may involve hierarchical syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer language models show evidence of structural priming.
Priming strength is boosted by semantic similarity and lexical overlap between prime and target sentences.
Priming effects persist but are asymmetrical when primes are semantically implausible.
Priming strength increases with recency (proximity) and cumulative exposure to the prime structure.
The structural representations may encode hierarchical syntactic information, as shown by priming with nested dependencies.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on only two syntactic alternations in English.
The corpus is template-based and may not capture naturalistic language.
Only auto-regressive language models are considered; masked LMs are not investigated.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to other syntactic constructions and languages.
Use more naturalistic data beyond template-based corpora.
Investigate structural priming in masked language models.
papers.abstract: Abstract We investigate the extent to which modern neural language models are susceptible to structural priming, the phenomenon whereby the structure of a sentence makes the same structure more probable in a follow-up sentence. We explore how priming can be used to study the potential of these models to learn abstract structural information, which is a prerequisite for good performance on tasks that require natural language understanding skills. We introduce a novel metric and release Prime-LM, a large corpus where we control for various linguistic factors that interact with priming strength. We find that Transformer models indeed show evidence of structural priming, but also that the generalizations they learned are to some extent modulated by semantic information. Our experiments also show that the representations acquired by the models may not only encode abstract sequential structure but involve certain level of hierarchical syntactic information. More generally, our study shows that the priming paradigm is a useful, additional tool for gaining insights into the capacities of language models and opens the door to future priming-based investigations that probe the model’s internal states.1

papers.title: Same Neurons, Different Languages: Probing Morphosyntax in Multilingual Pre-trained Models
papers.research_question: Does multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in the same subset of neurons across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual pre-trained models develop cross-lingually entangled representations of morphosyntax, with neuron overlap varying by category and influenced by language proximity and pre-training data size.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual pre-trained models implicitly align morphosyntactic information across languages by using overlapping subsets of neurons, which may affect their cross-lingual transfer capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Significant cross-lingual overlap exists in neurons encoding morphosyntactic information.
Overlap varies across morphosyntactic categories and is lower for categories with larger inventories of possible values.
Overlap is higher for languages within the same genus or with similar typological features.
Overlap increases with pre-training data size but decreases with larger model size (comparing XLM-R-base and XLM-R-large).
XLM-R-base tends to share more neurons than m-BERT for encoding morphosyntactic attributes.
future_direction: Artificially encouraging neuron overlap to facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual inference to low-resource and typologically distant languages.
papers.abstract: The success of multilingual pre-trained models is underpinned by their ability to learn representations shared by multiple languages even in absence of any explicit supervision. However, it remains unclear how these models learn to generalise across languages. In this work, we conjecture that multilingual pre-trained models can derive language-universal abstractions about grammar. In particular, we investigate whether morphosyntactic information is encoded in the same subset of neurons in different languages. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study over 43 languages and 14 morphosyntactic categories with a state-of-the-art neuron-level probe. Our findings show that the cross-lingual overlap between neurons is significant, but its extent may vary across categories and depends on language proximity and pre-training data size.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: Echoes of BERT: Do Modern Language Models Rediscover the Classical NLP Pipeline?
papers.research_question: How do modern language models encode linguistic structure, and do they rediscover the classical NLP pipeline observed in earlier models like BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: Do Language Models Associate Sound with Meaning? A Multimodal Study of Sound Symbolism
papers.research_question: How do Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) associate sound-symbolic words with semantic features similar to human phonetic intuition, and how do their internal attention patterns align with phonosemantic relationships?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that MLLMs exhibit phonetic intuitions aligning with linguistic research and that their internal attention patterns highlight focus on iconic phonemes, bridging AI and cognitive linguistics.
papers.conclusion: MLLMs demonstrate phonetic iconicity and internal attention mechanisms that reflect sound symbolism, providing insights into multimodal interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
MLLMs show phonetic intuition across multiple semantic dimensions, performing above baseline for both natural and constructed words.
Models have modality-specific preferences, using audio for acoustically grounded features and text for articulatory or visually driven features.
There are discrepancies between human and model performance, with models not fully aligning with human semantic alignment.
Attention analysis reveals that MLLMs attend to sound-symbolic phonemes, with higher attention in late layers for constructed words.
The constructed word group shows clearer phonosemantic attention patterns compared to natural words.
papers.limitation:
Discrepancies exist between human phonetic intuition and model performance, indicating models are not fully human-like in semantic alignment.
Models may overlook subtle phonosemantic cues due to training on large-scale distributional semantics of natural languages.
papers.abstract: Sound symbolism is a linguistic concept that refers to non-arbitrary associations between phonetic forms and their meanings. We suggest that this can be a compelling probe into how Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) interpret auditory information in human languages. We investigate MLLMs' performance on phonetic iconicity across textual (orthographic and IPA) and auditory forms of inputs with up to 25 semantic dimensions (e.g., sharp vs. round), observing models' layer-wise information processing by measuring phoneme-level attention fraction scores. To this end, we present LEX-ICON, an extensive mimetic word dataset consisting of 8,052 words from four natural languages (English, French, Japanese, and Korean) and 2,930 systematically constructed pseudo-words, annotated with semantic features applied across both text and audio modalities. Our key findings demonstrate (1) MLLMs' phonetic intuitions that align with existing linguistic research across multiple semantic dimensions and (2) phonosemantic attention patterns that highlight models' focus on iconic phonemes. These results bridge domains of artificial intelligence and cognitive linguistics, providing the first large-scale, quantitative analyses of phonetic iconicity in terms of MLLMs' interpretability.

papers.title: Behind the Scene: Revealing the Secrets of Pre-trained Vision-and-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained vision-and-language models work internally? Specifically, the paper investigates multimodal fusion, modality importance, cross-modal interaction, visual relations, and linguistic knowledge in these models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces VALUE, a set of probing tasks for vision-and-language models, and uses it to analyze UNITER and LXMERT, revealing that textual modality is more dominant, a subset of heads specialize in cross-modal interaction, and visual relations and linguistic knowledge are encoded.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into the inner workings of pre-trained V+L models and offers guidelines for future model design, such as preferring single-stream architecture and initializing with BERT weights.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models attend more to text than images during inference.
A subset of attention heads are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions.
Learned attention matrices show patterns coherent with latent alignment between image regions and textual words.
Attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions.
Linguistic knowledge is effectively encoded in the attention heads.
future_direction: Perform model compression via pruning attention heads based on the analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent Transformer-based large-scale pre-trained models have revolutionized vision-and-language (V+L) research. Models such as ViLBERT, LXMERT and UNITER have significantly lifted state of the art across a wide range of V+L benchmarks with joint image-text pre-training. However, little is known about the inner mechanisms that destine their impressive success. To reveal the secrets behind the scene of these powerful models, we present VALUE (Vision-And-Language Understanding Evaluation), a set of meticulously designed probing tasks (e.g., Visual Coreference Resolution, Visual Relation Detection, Linguistic Probing Tasks) generalizable to standard pre-trained V+L models, aiming to decipher the inner workings of multimodal pre-training (e.g., the implicit knowledge garnered in individual attention heads, the inherent cross-modal alignment learned through contextualized multimodal embeddings). Through extensive analysis of each archetypal model architecture via these probing tasks, our key observations are: (i) Pre-trained models exhibit a propensity for attending over text rather than images during inference. (ii) There exists a subset of attention heads that are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions. (iii) Learned attention matrix in pre-trained models demonstrates patterns coherent with the latent alignment between image regions and textual words. (iv) Plotted attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions. (v) Pure linguistic knowledge is also effectively encoded in the attention heads. These are valuable insights serving to guide future work towards designing better model architecture and objectives for multimodal pre-training.

papers.title: What Can an Accent Identifier Learn? Probing Phonetic and Prosodic Information in a Wav2vec2-based Accent Identification Model
papers.research_question: How does accent identification fine-tuning guide the representation change for phoneme and prosody information in a self-supervised learning model?
papers.core_contribution: The study shows that accent identification fine-tuning enhances phoneme and prosody representations in the top layers of Wav2vec 2.0, with similarities to ASR fine-tuning, and reveals accent-specific phoneme representations in layer 9.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into the distribution of phonetic and prosody knowledge in Wav2vec 2.0 and how an AID task affects such knowledge, with changes primarily in the top layers.
papers.key_findings:
AID fine-tuning mainly causes changes in the top 4 layers of the model.
The top 2 layers gain improved representations for both phoneme and prosody after fine-tuning.
Layer 9 shows strong accent-specific phoneme representations.
Prosody knowledge is enhanced in the top layers, with prominence information likely encoded in lower layers.
The pre-trained model already has good phoneme representations for US accent, which are maintained after fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: Limited number of speakers in the training data may cause over-fitting, especially for some accents.
future_direction: Analyses of other SSL models with different architectures and training objectives.
papers.abstract: This study is focused on understanding and quantifying the change in phoneme and prosody information encoded in the Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) model, brought by an accent identification (AID) fine-tuning task. This problem is addressed based on model probing. Specifically, we conduct a systematic layer-wise analysis of the representations of the Transformer layers on a phoneme correlation task, and a novel word-level prosody prediction task. We compare the probing performance of the pre-trained and fine-tuned SSL models. Results show that the AID fine-tuning task steers the top 2 layers to learn richer phoneme and prosody representation. These changes share some similarities with the effects of fine-tuning with an Automatic Speech Recognition task. In addition, we observe strong accent-specific phoneme representations in layer 9. To sum up, this study provides insights into the understanding of SSL features and their interactions with fine-tuning tasks.

papers.title: Probing Subphonemes in Morphology Models
papers.research_question: How well do transformers capture phonological and subphonemic features in morphological tasks, and how does this vary by feature type (local vs. long-distance) and language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that local phonological features are captured in phoneme embeddings, while long-distance features are better represented in the encoder's contextualized embeddings, and that this encoding depends on the feature's importance and locality in the language.
papers.conclusion: The degree to which phonological features are embedded in the transformer's representation depends on the feature's importance for the morphology and phonology of the language and on the locality of the feature's importance, with long-context features more salient in the encoder. These results help explain empirical training methods in morphological inflection.
papers.key_findings:
Local phonological features (e.g., final-obstruent devoicing in Turkish) are well captured in phoneme embeddings.
Long-distance phonological features (e.g., vowel harmony) are better represented in the encoder's contextualized embeddings.
The compression score (C) varies across features and languages, indicating how well phonological features are encoded.
The lemma copying model performs on par or better than the inflection model in the phoneme probe, possibly due to dataset noise.
The findings suggest that subphonemic features are already present in the representations, and transfer learning in morphological inflection might stem from the model's ability to acquire these approximately universal features.
papers.limitation:
The probing method might have underlying biases in its components: the transliteration tools, the character-based transformer, and the morphology inflection datasets' quality.
The study omitted data hallucination augmentation because it might indulge phonologically invalid words.
future_direction: Investigate the variance across languages and models.
papers.abstract: Transformers have achieved state-of-the-art performance in morphological inflection tasks, yet their ability to generalize across languages and morphological rules remains limited. One possible explanation for this behavior can be the degree to which these models are able to capture implicit phenomena at the phonological and subphonemic levels. We introduce a language-agnostic probing method to investigate phonological feature encoding in transformers trained directly on phonemes, and perform it across seven morphologically diverse languages. We show that phonological features which are local, such as final-obstruent devoicing in Turkish, are captured well in phoneme embeddings, whereas long-distance dependencies like vowel harmony are better represented in the transformer's encoder. Finally, we discuss how these findings inform empirical strategies for training morphological models, particularly regarding the role of subphonemic feature acquisition.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: FuxiTranyu: A Multilingual Large Language Model Trained with Balanced Data
papers.research_question: How to build a multilingual large language model with balanced data to mitigate performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FuxiTranyu, a multilingual LLM trained on balanced data, which shows competitive performance and more consistent multilingual representations compared to existing models.
papers.conclusion: FuxiTranyu is a strong open-source multilingual LLM, and balanced pre-training data is crucial for achieving consistent multilingual representations and performance.
papers.key_findings:
FuxiTranyu outperforms previous multilingual LLMs like BLOOM-7B1 and PolyLM-13B on several multilingual benchmarks.
Balanced pre-training data leads to more consistent multilingual representations across languages.
Neuron analysis reveals that deep layers are more language-specific and the importance of attention and MLP components varies across layers.
Languages with extremely limited resources (e.g., Bengali, Tamil) are allocated fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model achieves high performance on summarization tasks, outperforming baseline models on XL-Sum.
papers.limitation:
Languages with extremely limited resources, such as Bengali and Tamil, are allocated with fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model underperforms in some tasks (e.g., m-ARC, m-MMLU) due to limited training data for English.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated prowess in a wide range of tasks. However, many LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages. To mitigate this challenge, we present FuxiTranyu, an open-source multilingual LLM, which is designed to satisfy the need of the research community for balanced and high-performing multilingual capabilities. The base model, FuxiTranyu-8B, features 8 billion parameters and is trained from scratch on meticulously balanced multilingual data that contains 600 billion tokens covering 43 natural languages and 16 programming languages. We also develop two instruction-tuned models: FuxiTranyu-8B-SFT which is fine-tuned on a diverse multilingual instruction dataset, and FuxiTranyu-8B-DPO which is further refined with DPO on a preference dataset for enhanced alignment ability. Extensive experiments on a wide range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate the competitive performance of FuxiTranyu against existing multilingual LLMs, e.g., BLOOM-7B, PolyLM-13B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Both neuron and representation interpretability analyses reveal that FuxiTranyu achieves consistent multilingual representations across languages. To promote further research into multilingual LLMs, we release both the base and instruction-tuned FuxiTranyu models together with 58 pre-training checkpoints at HuggingFace (see https://huggingface.co/TJUNLP/FuxiTranyu-8B) and Github (see https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/FuxiTranyu).

papers.title: Compositional Processing Emerges in Neural Networks Solving Math Problems
papers.research_question: Do deep neural networks evaluate arithmetic expressions using the principle of compositionality by encoding and combining partial results?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on math problems can encode partial results of sub-expressions in their internal representations, demonstrating emergent compositional processing.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can exhibit compositional processing when trained on math problems, though imperfectly, suggesting a blend of compositional and holistic strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode digit quantities in their representations, with vectors organized by numerical value.
Operators encode intermediate arithmetic results, with vector distances correlating with value differences.
These encodings are found in attention vectors, indicating compositional processing.
Compositionality is imperfect, as shown by non-zero correlations across sequences.
Both standard and TP-Transformers exhibit similar patterns of compositional encoding.
papers.limitation:
The observed compositionality is imperfect, with non-zero correlations indicating incomplete separation of sub-expressions.
Models show poor generalization on extrapolation problems with different surface features.
future_direction: Clarify whether scaling leads to human-level compositionality or if explicit design is needed.
papers.abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science concerns the learning mechanisms underlying compositionality in human cognition. Humans can infer the structured relationships (e.g., grammatical rules) implicit in their sensory observations (e.g., auditory speech), and use this knowledge to guide the composition of simpler meanings into complex wholes. Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: Are Representations Built from the Ground Up? An Empirical Examination of Local Composition in Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether modern language models learn to represent both compositional and non-compositional phrases, and whether their internal representations align with human judgments of compositionality.
papers.core_contribution: The representation of a parent phrase can be predicted with some accuracy using an affine transformation of its children's representations, but this predictability does not correlate well with human judgments of semantic compositionality, indicating language models may not accurately distinguish between compositional and non-compositional phrases.
papers.conclusion: Language model representations have an effective affine approximation in terms of a phrase's syntactic children, but human compositionality judgments do not align well with how these representations are structured, suggesting a need for improved compositional generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Parent phrase representations can be predicted with reasonable accuracy using an affine transformation of child representations.
There are significant differences in compositionality across phrase types (e.g., named entities are less compositional).
Longer phrases tend to be more compositionally represented in average embeddings but not in CLS representations.
Human judgments of compositionality do not strongly correlate with model compositionality scores.
Models perform poorly at identifying which subphrase contributes more to meaning and at distinguishing idioms from non-idioms.
papers.limitation:
The study was conducted on a relatively small set of English language models.
Analyses depend on the definition of child constituents, which may be harder for languages that differ substantially from English.
The work provides a diagnostic but not a mechanistic understanding of model behavior.
The work does not provide a clear avenue to fix the identified problem.
future_direction: Investigate the evolution of compositionality through training.
Motivate methods that allow LMs to achieve improved compositional generalization while representing non-compositionality.
Understand what data distributions or training methods encourage model representations to be more aligned with human judgments.
papers.abstract: Compositionality, the phenomenon where the meaning of a phrase can be derived from its constituent parts, is a hallmark of human language. At the same time, many phrases are non-compositional, carrying a meaning beyond that of each part in isolation. Representing both of these types of phrases is critical for language understanding, but it is an open question whether modern language models (LMs) learn to do so; in this work we examine this question. We first formulate a problem of predicting the LM-internal representations of longer phrases given those of their constituents. We find that the representation of a parent phrase can be predicted with some accuracy given an affine transformation of its children. While we would expect the predictive accuracy to correlate with human judgments of semantic compositionality, we find this is largely not the case, indicating that LMs may not accurately distinguish between compositional and non-compositional phrases. We perform a variety of analyses, shedding light on when different varieties of LMs do and do not generate compositional representations, and discuss implications for future modeling work.

papers.title: Analyzing the Structure of Attention in a Transformer Language Model
papers.research_question: Does attention align with syntactic dependency relations? Which attention heads attend to which part-of-speech tags? How does attention capture long-distance relationships versus short-distance ones?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes attention in the GPT-2 Transformer language model, finding that attention heads specialize in particular part-of-speech tags at different layers, attention aligns with dependency relations most strongly in middle layers, and the deepest layers capture the most distant relationships.
papers.conclusion: The structure of attention in GPT-2 is closely tied to the language modeling objective, with attention patterns often focusing on words relevant for predicting the next token. The analysis provides human-interpretable descriptions of model behavior and is complementary to linguistic probing approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Attention targets different parts of speech at different layer depths within the model.
Attention aligns with dependency relations most strongly in the middle layers.
The deepest layers of the model capture the most distant relationships.
Attention heads exhibit specific patterns, such as focusing on acronyms, place names, or head nouns, as revealed by exemplar sentences.
Attention variability distinguishes content-dependent from content-independent (position-based) heads.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Wikipedia text, which has a specific encyclopedic format and style, so it is unclear how attention patterns manifest in other types of content.
Attention may not fully explain individual model predictions, as noted by recent work (Jain and Wallace, 2019).
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other Transformer models such as BERT, which has a bidirectional architecture and is trained on both token-level and sentence-level tasks.
Analyze attention patterns in other types of content, such as dialog scripts or song lyrics.
Analyze attention patterns in longer texts, especially for new Transformer variants like Transformer-XL and Sparse Transformer.
papers.abstract: The Transformer is a fully attention-based alternative to recurrent networks that has achieved state-of-the-art results across a range of NLP tasks. In this paper, we analyze the structure of attention in a Transformer language model, the GPT-2 small pretrained model. We visualize attention for individual instances and analyze the interaction between attention and syntax over a large corpus. We find that attention targets different parts of speech at different layer depths within the model, and that attention aligns with dependency relations most strongly in the middle layers. We also find that the deepest layers of the model capture the most distant relationships. Finally, we extract exemplar sentences that reveal highly specific patterns targeted by particular attention heads.

papers.title: How do Multimodal Foundation Models Encode Text and Speech? An Analysis of Cross-Lingual and Cross-Modal Representations
papers.research_question: How do multimodal foundation models encode text and speech? Specifically, how do they represent semantically equivalent sentences across languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes cross-lingual and cross-modal representations in multimodal foundation models, finding that cross-modal similarity increases over layers, length adaptation helps but is limited to high-resource languages, speech has larger cross-lingual differences than text, and the modality gap is often larger than the language gap.
papers.conclusion: While multimodal foundation models present a unified architecture, they do not inherently create fully unified semantic representations. Representational gaps such as speech-text length mismatches, weak representations for low-resource languages, and tokenizer bottlenecks persist.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal representations converge over model layers, except in the initial layers which are specialized for text or speech processing.
Length adaptation mechanisms (e.g., pooling, Q-Former) are crucial for reducing the cross-modal gap, but their effectiveness is primarily limited to high-resource languages.
Speech exhibits larger cross-lingual differences than text, likely due to greater variability in acoustic features and recording conditions.
For models not explicitly trained for modality-agnostic representations (Seamless, SALMONN), the modality gap is more prominent than the language gap.
Tokenizer fragmentation for languages with diverse scripts (e.g., in SALMONN) leads to inflated initial similarity scores that drop in subsequent layers.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on the FLEURS dataset, which is created from Wikipedia texts, may limit generalizability to other domains like informal or spoken texts.
The study focuses only on speech and text modalities; exploring other modalities like images is out of scope.
Only three multimodal foundation models are analyzed; newer models like Qwen-Audio and Llama 3 are not covered.
Six of the 30 analyzed languages are not shared between SONAR and the other models, creating a non-fully overlapping experimental setup.
Findings are based on intrinsic analyses (SVCCA on activations); other explainability methods or downstream task performance could provide complementary insights.
papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models aim to create a unified representation space that abstracts away from surface features like language syntax or modality differences. To investigate this, we study the internal representations of three recent models, analyzing the model activations from semantically equivalent sentences across languages in the text and speech modalities. Our findings reveal that: 1) Cross-modal representations converge over model layers, except in the initial layers specialized at text and speech processing. 2) Length adaptation is crucial for reducing the cross-modal gap between text and speech, although current approaches' effectiveness is primarily limited to high-resource languages. 3) Speech exhibits larger cross-lingual differences than text. 4) For models not explicitly trained for modality-agnostic representations, the modality gap is more prominent than the language gap.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How and where do multilingual language models encode syntactic agreement? Are neurons shared across languages and structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends causal probing to multilingual language models, finding two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement depending on distance, significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual models but not masked language models, and that behavioral analyses underestimate masked language models' sensitivity to syntax.
papers.conclusion: Causal probing reveals distinct mechanisms for short- and long-range syntactic agreement in multilingual models, with autoregressive models showing more cross-lingual neuron sharing than masked models, and suggests that models encode syntax similarly across languages but with language-specific neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement: one for short-range (adjacent subject-verb) and one for long-range (separated by other tokens).
Neurons are shared across syntactic structures but not with semantic baselines, indicating abstract syntactic agreement encoding.
In autoregressive language models (XGLM), there is significant neuron overlap across languages, but in masked language models (mBERT), neurons are rarely shared across languages.
Neuron sparsity differs across structures (more sparse for short-range agreement) but not across languages.
Behavioral analyses likely underestimate how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information because negative interference from other neurons masks strong syntax-sensitive neurons.
papers.limitation:
Limited to stimuli where subjects and verbs are single tokens, restricting the range of words and languages that can be studied.
Probing individual neurons may oversimplify because complex phenomena like syntactic agreement are likely encoded in sets of neurons.
future_direction: Developing methods for multi-token interventions and variable-length sequences.
Probing multiple neurons simultaneously to causally implicate model regions rather than individual components.
Investigating redundantly encoded syntactic information across neurons.
papers.abstract: Structural probing work has found evidence for latent syntactic information in pre-trained language models. However, much of this analysis has focused on monolingual models, and analyses of multilingual models have employed correlational methods that are confounded by the choice of probing tasks. In this study, we causally probe multilingual language models (XGLM and multilingual BERT) as well as monolingual BERT-based models across various languages; we do this by performing counterfactual perturbations on neuron activations and observing the effect on models' subject-verb agreement probabilities. We observe where in the model and to what extent syntactic agreement is encoded in each language. We find significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual language models, but not masked language models. We also find two distinct layer-wise effect patterns and two distinct sets of neurons used for syntactic agreement, depending on whether the subject and verb are separated by other tokens. Finally, we find that behavioral analyses of language models are likely underestimating how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information.

papers.title: That Looks Hard: Characterizing Linguistic Complexity in Humans and Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the relationship between online (eye-tracking) and offline (human judgment) measures of sentence complexity and how they are modeled in a neural language model.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a comprehensive analysis of linguistic phenomena correlated with eye-tracking and human complexity judgments, compares feature-based and neural models for predicting complexity, and shows that fine-tuning a language model on complexity tasks leads to increased encoding of relevant linguistic properties in its representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates a connection between eye-tracking metrics and explicit complexity perception, shows comparable performance between feature-based and neural models, and finds that fine-tuning on complexity tasks leads to the natural emergence of task-related linguistic properties in the model's representations, suggesting a link between acquired linguistic knowledge and downstream task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Sentence length is the most correlated predictor for all complexity metrics, but other linguistic features also contribute.
When controlling for sentence length, online and offline complexity metrics show different correlations with linguistic features.
ALBERT performs on par with an SVM using explicit linguistic features for predicting complexity, suggesting it implicitly learns relevant linguistic properties.
Probing experiments show that fine-tuning on complexity tasks increases the model's encoding of complexity-related linguistic features in its representations.
The model's linguistic competencies acquired during training are interpretable and related to its predictive performance on complexity tasks.
papers.limitation:
The fine-tuning corpora are small in size.
The SVM model with explicit features performs poorly on larger length bins, likely due to limited data affecting generalization.
future_direction: Test the effectiveness of tasks inspired by human language learning as intermediate steps to train more robust and parsimonious neural language models.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between two complementary perspectives in the human assessment of sentence complexity and how they are modeled in a neural language model (NLM). The first perspective takes into account multiple online behavioral metrics obtained from eye-tracking recordings. The second one concerns the offline perception of complexity measured by explicit human judgments. Using a broad spectrum of linguistic features modeling lexical, morpho-syntactic, and syntactic properties of sentences, we perform a comprehensive analysis of linguistic phenomena associated with the two complexity viewpoints and report similarities and differences. We then show the effectiveness of linguistic features when explicitly leveraged by a regression model for predicting sentence complexity and compare its results with the ones obtained by a fine-tuned neural language model. We finally probe the NLM's linguistic competence before and after fine-tuning, highlighting how linguistic information encoded in representations changes when the model learns to predict complexity.

papers.title: A Compositional Neural Architecture for Language
papers.research_question: How can hierarchical structure and compositionality in language be reconciled with principles from cell assembly computation in neuroscience?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a neural architecture based on multidimensional coordinate systems and gain modulation to explain how the brain achieves compositional and hierarchical language processing.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a neural architecture that unifies insights from linguistics, psycholinguistics, and neuroscience to explain how the brain achieves compositional language processing through gain modulation and neural oscillations.
papers.key_findings:
The neural architecture uses a manifold of neural trajectories to encode sensory, motor, and abstract linguistic states.
Gain modulation, including inhibition, tunes the path in the manifold and infers latent structure.
Predictive information about upcoming sensory input during production and comprehension is available without a separate operation.
The architecture synthesizes neural entrainment to speech, systems neuroscience, category theory, and a symbolic-connectionist computational model (DORA) that uses time and rhythm.
The proposal moves toward unifying insights from linguistics and psycholinguistics with neural computation.
papers.abstract: Hierarchical structure and compositionality imbue human language with unparalleled expressive power and set it apart from other perception-action systems. However, neither formal nor neurobiological models account for how these defining computational properties might arise in a physiological system. I attempt to reconcile hierarchy and compositionality with principles from cell assembly computation in neuroscience; the result is an emerging theory of how the brain could convert distributed perceptual representations into hierarchical structures across multiple timescales while representing interpretable incremental stages of (de)compositional meaning. The model's architecture-a multidimensional coordinate system based on neurophysiological models of sensory processing-proposes that a manifold of neural trajectories encodes sensory, motor, and abstract linguistic states. Gain modulation, including inhibition, tunes the path in the manifold in accordance with behavior and is how latent structure is inferred. As a consequence, predictive information about upcoming sensory input during production and comprehension is available without a separate operation. The proposed processing mechanism is synthesized from current models of neural entrainment to speech, concepts from systems neuroscience and category theory, and a symbolic-connectionist computational model that uses time and rhythm to structure information. I build on evidence from cognitive neuroscience and computational modeling that suggests a formal and mechanistic alignment between structure building and neural oscillations, and moves toward unifying basic insights from linguistics and psycholinguistics with the currency of neural computation.

papers.title: What Are Large Language Models Mapping to in the Brain? A Case Against Over-Reliance on Brain Scores
papers.research_question: What are large language models mapping to in the brain? The paper questions whether high brain scores indicate shared computational principles between LLMs and human language processing or are explained by simpler, theoretically uninteresting features.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that high brain scores of LLMs on neural datasets can be largely explained by simple features like sentence length, position, and static word embeddings, cautioning against over-interpreting these scores as evidence of shared computational principles with human language processing.
papers.conclusion: Brain scores on the analyzed datasets should be interpreted with caution, and analyses using brain scores should be accompanied by a systematic deconstruction of neural encoding performance against simple features to avoid over-interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Shuffled train-test splits are severely affected by temporal autocorrelation, and a trivial feature (OASM) that encodes this autocorrelation outperforms LLMs and accounts for most of their explained neural variance.
Untrained GPT2-XL's brain score is fully accounted for by two simple features: sentence length and sentence position.
Trained GPT2-XL's brain score is largely explained by sentence length, sentence position, and static word embeddings; only a small additional amount is explained by sense embeddings and contextual syntactic representations.
On the Fedorenko dataset, word position explains all of the untrained and most of the trained GPT2-XL neural predictivity.
On the Blank dataset, GPT2-XL predicts neural activity at chance levels when using contiguous train-test splits.
papers.limitation:
The method of examining how much neural variance an LLM predicts over simple features scales poorly when the number of feature spaces is large.
The procedure may be biased against regressions with many feature spaces due to noise in neural data and low sample sizes.
The study did not analyze datasets with large amounts of neural data per participant, where the gap between simple and complex features might be larger.
papers.abstract: Given the remarkable capabilities of large language models (LLMs), there has been a growing interest in evaluating their similarity to the human brain. One approach towards quantifying this similarity is by measuring how well a model predicts neural signals, also called "brain score". Internal representations from LLMs achieve state-of-the-art brain scores, leading to speculation that they share computational principles with human language processing. This inference is only valid if the subset of neural activity predicted by LLMs reflects core elements of language processing. Here, we question this assumption by analyzing three neural datasets used in an impactful study on LLM-to-brain mappings, with a particular focus on an fMRI dataset where participants read short passages. We first find that when using shuffled train-test splits, as done in previous studies with these datasets, a trivial feature that encodes temporal autocorrelation not only outperforms LLMs but also accounts for the majority of neural variance that LLMs explain. We therefore use contiguous splits moving forward. Second, we explain the surprisingly high brain scores of untrained LLMs by showing they do not account for additional neural variance beyond two simple features: sentence length and sentence position. This undermines evidence used to claim that the transformer architecture biases computations to be more brain-like. Third, we find that brain scores of trained LLMs on this dataset can largely be explained by sentence length, position, and pronoun-dereferenced static word embeddings; a small, additional amount is explained by sense-specific embeddings and contextual representations of sentence structure. We conclude that over-reliance on brain scores can lead to over-interpretations of similarity between LLMs and brains, and emphasize the importance of deconstructing what LLMs are mapping to in neural signals.

papers.title: Language Embeddings Sometimes Contain Typological Generalizations
papers.research_question: To what extent can neural network models learn generalizations about language structure, and how do we find out what they have learned? Which typological features can be discovered when the system is not told what to look for?
papers.core_contribution: This paper finds that neural models can sometimes learn typological generalizations in their language representations, but less readily than suggested by prior work, and that careful evaluation is essential to avoid false positives. It also releases several resources for 1295 languages.
papers.conclusion: Neural models can discover typological generalizations, but they do so less readily than suggested by previous research, and careful evaluation is necessary to confirm such discoveries.
papers.key_findings:
Some generalizations in learned language representations are surprisingly close to traditional typological features, but most models (including those from previous work) do not appear to have made linguistically meaningful generalizations.
Careful attention to evaluation details, such as controlling for genealogical and areal correlations, is essential to avoid false positives.
The word-level language model (WordLM) captures word order features and some morphological features, while many other models (including MTVec, MTCell, and Ö&T) show little evidence of encoding typological features when evaluated with their method.
Lexical baselines (ASJP and Lexical similarity vectors) do not encode structural features, as expected, and can serve as a baseline for evaluation.
papers.limitation: The study only tries to connect neural language representations with known features from the typological literature, not with potentially novel generalizations.
future_direction: Investigating whether models make typological generalizations that human linguists have not previously made.
papers.abstract: To what extent can neural network models learn generalizations about language structure, and how do we find out what they have learned? We explore these questions by training neural models for a range of natural language processing tasks on a massively multilingual dataset of Bible translations in 1295 languages. The learned language representations are then compared to existing typological databases as well as to a novel set of quantitative syntactic and morphological features obtained through annotation projection. We conclude that some generalizations are surprisingly close to traditional features from linguistic typology, but that most of our models, as well as those of previous work, do not appear to have made linguistically meaningful generalizations. Careful attention to details in the evaluation turns out to be essential to avoid false positives. Furthermore, to encourage continued work in this field, we release several resources covering most or all of the languages in our data: (i) multiple sets of language representations, (ii) multilingual word embeddings, (iii) projected and predicted syntactic and morphological features, (iv) software to provide linguistically sound evaluations of language representations.

papers.title: Joint processing of linguistic properties in brains and language models
papers.research_question: What linguistic properties are responsible for the alignment between brain recordings (fMRI) and language model representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a direct approach to evaluate joint linguistic processing in brains and language models by removing specific linguistic properties from model representations, showing this significantly decreases brain alignment, with syntactic properties having the largest effect.
papers.conclusion: The direct approach provides clear evidence that specific linguistic information, particularly syntactic properties, underlies the alignment between brain and language models, opening new avenues for mapping joint information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Removing each tested linguistic property (surface, syntactic, semantic) results in a significant decrease in brain alignment across all layers of BERT and GPT-2.
Syntactic properties (Top Constituents and Tree Depth) have the largest effect on the trend of brain alignment across model layers.
Top Constituents affects alignment in all language brain regions, while Tree Depth specifically affects temporal (ATL, PTL) and frontal (IFG, MFG) regions.
Semantic properties (Tense, Subject Number, Object Number) affect alignment more specifically in regions like the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC).
The method reveals that different linguistic properties are important for alignment in different brain regions and sub-regions.
papers.limitation:
The removal approach may also remove information correlated with the removed linguistic property due to dataset limitations.
Substantial brain alignment remains after removing all tested properties, indicating not all relevant linguistic properties have been accounted for.
The study is limited to English language stimuli and two language models (BERT and GPT-2).
future_direction: Incorporate additional linguistic properties to fully characterize joint processing.
Investigate larger language models beyond BERT and GPT-2.
Extend the approach to languages beyond English.
papers.abstract: Language models have been shown to be very effective in predicting brain recordings of subjects experiencing complex language stimuli. For a deeper understanding of this alignment, it is important to understand the correspondence between the detailed processing of linguistic information by the human brain versus language models. We investigate this correspondence via a direct approach, in which we eliminate information related to specific linguistic properties in the language model representations and observe how this intervention affects the alignment with fMRI brain recordings obtained while participants listened to a story. We investigate a range of linguistic properties (surface, syntactic, and semantic) and find that the elimination of each one results in a significant decrease in brain alignment. Specifically, we find that syntactic properties (i.e. Top Constituents and Tree Depth) have the largest effect on the trend of brain alignment across model layers. These findings provide clear evidence for the role of specific linguistic information in the alignment between brain and language models, and open new avenues for mapping the joint information processing in both systems. We make the code publicly available [https://github.com/subbareddy248/linguistic-properties-brain-alignment].

papers.title: Attention weights accurately predict language representations in the brain
papers.research_question: Are attention weights in Transformer-based language models related to language representations in the brain? Can attention weights predict brain responses to language stimuli?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights from Transformer-based language models accurately predict brain responses in language-related cortical areas, and contain information not captured by lexical or contextual embeddings.
papers.conclusion: Attention weights in Transformer-based LMs capture information that is reflected in brain representations during language processing, and indicate cortical areas that could be involved in integrating context across words.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 accurately predict brain responses in frontal and temporal cortices associated with language processing.
Attention weights better predict brain responses than lexical embeddings in many language-related areas.
Attention weights from middle layers of BERT explain the most variance in brain responses, consistent with linguistic relevance of middle layers.
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 perform similarly in predicting brain responses, suggesting consistency across unidirectional and bidirectional models.
In some cortical areas, attention weights predict brain responses better than contextual embeddings, indicating additional information in attention weights.
papers.limitation:
The temporal resolution of fMRI (2s) does not capture all the rapid changes in human speech.
Analyses were limited to English language comprehension.
The analyses demonstrate similarity of representations between Transformer-based LMs and brain responses, but do not directly prove the existence of similar underlying computational mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply the methods to other languages to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of context integration in the brain and in artificial neural networks.

Compare the results of our method of computing attention weights with more cognitively-inspired methods to provide more specific insights into how attention weights in Transformer-based LMs relate to processes in the human brain.
papers.abstract: In Transformer-based language models (LMs) the attention mechanism converts token embeddings into contextual embeddings that incorporate information from neighboring words. The resulting contextual hidden state embeddings have enabled highly accurate models of brain responses, suggesting that the attention mechanism constructs contextual embeddings that carry information reflected in language-related brain representations. However, it is unclear whether the attention weights that are used to integrate information across words are themselves related to language representations in the brain. To address this question we analyzed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) recordings of participants reading English language narratives. We provided the narrative text as input to two LMs (BERT and GPT-2) and extracted their corresponding attention weights. We then used encoding models to determine how well attention weights can predict recorded brain responses. We find that attention weights accurately predict brain responses in much of the frontal and temporal cortices. Our results suggest that the attention mechanism itself carries information that is reflected in brain representations. Moreover, these results indicate cortical areas in which context integration may occur.

papers.title: Finding Structure in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to humans, and how can such structures be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that language models capture abstract linguistic structure similar to humans, and develops interpretability techniques to reveal this structure. It shows that models exhibit structural priming, generalize from indirect evidence, and that interpretability methods must be evaluated with care.
papers.conclusion: The thesis provides a detailed account of grammatical knowledge in language models and offers directions for using computational methods to investigate linguistic questions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit human-like structural priming effects, indicating they capture abstract syntactic structure.
Language models can generalize linguistic patterns from indirect evidence, as shown by filtered corpus training experiments.
Interpretability methods for feature interaction detection vary in faithfulness and must be evaluated carefully.
Language models use monotonicity information to predict negative polarity item licensing.
Adjective order preferences in language models are influenced by data statistics and cognitive factors.
papers.abstract: When we speak, write or listen, we continuously make predictions based on our knowledge of a language's grammar. Remarkably, children acquire this grammatical knowledge within just a few years, enabling them to understand and generalise to novel constructions that have never been uttered before. Language models are powerful tools that create representations of language by incrementally predicting the next word in a sentence, and they have had a tremendous societal impact in recent years. The central research question of this thesis is whether these models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to that of humans. This question lies at the intersection of natural language processing, linguistics, and interpretability. To address it, we will develop novel interpretability techniques that enhance our understanding of the complex nature of large-scale language models. We approach our research question from three directions. First, we explore the presence of abstract linguistic information through structural priming, a key paradigm in psycholinguistics for uncovering grammatical structure in human language processing. Next, we examine various linguistic phenomena, such as adjective order and negative polarity items, and connect a model's comprehension of these phenomena to the data distribution on which it was trained. Finally, we introduce a controlled testbed for studying hierarchical structure in language models using various synthetic languages of increasing complexity and examine the role of feature interactions in modelling this structure. Our findings offer a detailed account of the grammatical knowledge embedded in language model representations and provide several directions for investigating fundamental linguistic questions using computational methods.

papers.title: Learning Music Helps You Read: Using Transfer to Study Linguistic Structure in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does training on non-linguistic data with latent structure (like music or code) affect the ability of LSTMs to model natural language, and what structural features are being transferred?
papers.core_contribution: LSTMs can learn generalizable structural features from non-linguistic data (music, code) and transfer them to natural language, and hierarchical recursion is not necessary for this transfer; flat head-dependent pair structure is equally effective. Transfer between natural languages is correlated with syntactic typological similarity.
papers.conclusion: LSTMs can learn and transfer structural features from non-linguistic data to natural language, and simple head-dependent pair structure (not necessarily hierarchical) is sufficient for such transfer, suggesting recursion may not be as central to language learning as previously thought.
papers.key_findings:
Training on non-linguistic structured data (music, code) improves transfer to natural language compared to random baselines.
Training on artificial languages with nested hierarchical structure (Nesting Parentheses) and flat paired structure (Flat Parentheses) both lead to similar gains, indicating that recursion is not necessary for transfer.
Transfer performance between natural languages is highly correlated with typological syntactic similarity (WALS-syntax distance).
Vocabulary distribution (Zipfian) alone provides minor gains but structural features are far more important.
The TILT method provides a way to analyze structural inductive biases in language models.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to LSTM models; it is unknown if the results generalize to Transformer architectures.
The typological distance metric is based on only 49 syntactic features and may not be perfectly accurate.
future_direction: Test if the results hold on Transformer architectures.
Ablate specific structural features by creating hypothetical languages that differ in single grammatical features.
Test on structured data that's completely unrelated to language, such as images.
papers.abstract: We propose transfer learning as a method for analyzing the encoding of grammatical structure in neural language models. We train LSTMs on non-linguistic data and evaluate their performance on natural language to assess which kinds of data induce generalizable structural features that LSTMs can use for natural language. We find that training on non-linguistic data with latent structure (MIDI music or Java code) improves test performance on natural language, despite no overlap in surface form or vocabulary. To pinpoint the kinds of abstract structure that models may be encoding to lead to this improvement, we run similar experiments with two artificial parentheses languages: one which has a hierarchical recursive structure, and a control which has paired tokens but no recursion. Surprisingly, training a model on either of these artificial languages leads to the same substantial gains when testing on natural language. Further experiments on transfer between natural languages controlling for vocabulary overlap show that zero-shot performance on a test language is highly correlated with typological syntactic similarity to the training language, suggesting that representations induced by pre-training correspond to the cross-linguistic syntactic properties. Our results provide insights into the ways that neural models represent abstract syntactic structure, and also about the kind of structural inductive biases which allow for natural language acquisition.

papers.title: Language Models Learn POS First
papers.research_question: How and when are linguistic structures, such as part-of-speech tagging and global topic information, acquired during the training of language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that during training, language models acquire part-of-speech tagging early and global topic information continuously, using methods like gradient concentration and SVCCA.
papers.conclusion: Early training focuses on learning part-of-speech syntax for initial performance, while later training shifts to refining global topic representations for further gains.
papers.key_findings:
Frequent words have more concentrated gradients, and concentration increases over time during training.
Closed POS classes (e.g., pronouns, prepositions) show early concentration stabilization, while open classes (e.g., nouns, verbs) continue to become more concentrated.
Part-of-speech tagging is learned early in training, with representation peaking before the first optimizer step size rescale.
